guide.title: About JPEG compression
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPEG file?

Its name is short for the Joint Photographic Experts Group, which began its work in 1986. JPEG is lossy and made for photos. ITU-T standardized it as T.81 in 1992, and ISO as 10918-1 in 1994. Cameras and scanners write it, and every major browser can show it. The idea is to keep what the eye notices and drop what it doesn't. First the picture is split into small 8x8 pixel squares; a discrete cosine transform turns each square into frequencies, and Huffman coding packs the remainder.

The quality number controls how much of the fine detail is rounded off. A high quality keeps almost everything and makes a big file; a lower one rounds harder and the file shrinks. Quality is usually a 0 to 100 scale, though two programs given the same number can write different files. GIMP's default is 85.

Some arithmetic shows why the setting matters. A 12-megapixel photo is 12 million pixels with three color values each, about 36 MB before compression. Typical settings, a tenth to a twentieth of that, land between 1.8 and 3.6 MB.

The endings .jpg and .jpeg stand for one format, with image/jpeg as its media type, and US patent protection for it ended on 27 October 2006.

Compressing a JPEG that already exists means decoding it to pixels and encoding those pixels again with harder rounding. Progressive order is another way to save a JPEG: a blurry first pass appears, then detail fills in as the rest downloads.

### Programs that compress JPEG files

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- GIMP: the JPEG export dialog offers Quality, Progressive and Optimize settings.
- ImageMagick: reads JPG files in a terminal window.

**Mac**

- Preview: re-exports a JPEG with an adjustable quality.
- Photos: exports a batch of photos as JPEG, with JPEG Quality and Size choices.

**Web**

- Firefox: shows JPEG files.
- This page: MozJPEG at a fixed quality of 82, with several files at once.

**Web and Mobile**

- Chrome: shows JPEG files.

**Mobile**

- Safari: shows JPEG files.

### Original and compressed JPEG compared

- **Quality**: the copy is saved at quality 82, with no slider. Another program's 82 may not match it.
- **Progressive order**: the copy is a progressive JPEG, so a viewer can paint a rough picture first.
- **Metadata**: EXIF, XMP and the ICC color profile are left out. The decoded pixels are all that is encoded.
- **Orientation**: the EXIF orientation tag is not applied and not kept.
- **Pixel size**: the width and height don't change.
- **What stays the same**: the result is still image/jpeg, with 8 bits per color channel and no transparency or layers.
- **When the copy isn't smaller**: you get your original file back.

### Other ways to compress a JPEG

- **Preview (Mac):** go to File > Export, switch the Format pop-up menu to JPEG, move the quality control, then click Save.
- **Photos (Mac):** open File > Export > Export Photos, choose JPEG in the Photo Kind menu, reveal the options with the arrow beside it and reduce JPEG Quality or Size, then click Export.
- **GIMP (Linux, Mac and Windows):** pick File > Export As (Shift+Ctrl+E), choose JPEG, and in its dialog reduce Quality from the 85 it starts at.

### Problems with JPEG files

- **A form rejects .jpeg but takes .jpg**: the format is the same. Rename the ending, or convert with the [JPEG to JPG converter](/jpeg-to-jpg/).
- **The file is still too large after compressing**: this page changes only the quality. Resize the picture in an editor, then compress again.
- **A logo lost its transparent background**: JPEG has no alpha channel. Keep such images as PNG or WebP, and shrink a WebP with the [WebP compressor](/compress-webp/).
- **The compressor returned the file unchanged**: the new encode wasn't smaller than your file.
- **The photo is rotated wrongly**: the copy no longer carries its orientation tag. Apply the rotation in an editor first.
- **The camera details are missing**: EXIF isn't in the copy. Keep your original for the date and location.
- **Colors look different**: the ICC profile stays behind in your original. Keep it when color accuracy matters.
- **Many files at once**: pick them together, and each is compressed in turn and downloads as its own JPEG, with no ZIP to unpack.
- **Squares appear after many rounds**: detail is lost at each save. Return to the original instead of squeezing an already compressed file.

guide.title: About JPG compression
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPG file?

Work on JPEG began in 1986 with the Joint Photographic Experts Group, whose initials give the format its name. T.81, the ITU-T text from 1992, and ISO/IEC 10918-1, adopted in 1994, define its core standard. Cameras and scanners commonly produce it, all major browsers show it, and the US patents that covered it ran out on 27 October 2006. Both .jpg and .jpeg are the same format, and image/jpeg is its media type.

Baseline JPEG is lossy. The picture is grouped into 8x8 blocks; a discrete cosine transform is applied to every block, and Huffman coding packs the result as the finest detail is rounded off. The quality number says how coarse that rounding is. The scale commonly spans 0 to 100, yet one program's 80 need not match another's; GIMP starts at 85. A picture saved at ordinary settings is typically a tenth to a twentieth the size it would be uncompressed.

In a JPG each color channel is 8 bits wide, and neither an alpha channel nor layers exist. Progressive mode is optional: a rough picture shows first and gains detail while the rest of the file arrives. Compressing a JPG means decoding it and saving it again at a lower quality, which is a new lossy save.

### Programs that compress JPG files

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- GIMP: its JPEG export dialog has a Quality setting that defaults to 85, Progressive and Optimize options, and a choice of which metadata to keep.
- ImageMagick: reads JPG files from the command line.

**Mac**

- Preview: File > Export saves a JPEG and lets you adjust its quality.
- Photos: File > Export > Export Photos offers a JPEG Quality and a Size choice.

**Web**

- Firefox: displays JPG files.
- This page: MozJPEG at quality 82, run by your browser.

**Web and Mobile**

- Chrome: displays JPG files.

**Mobile**

- Safari: displays JPG files.

### Original and compressed JPG compared

- **Format**: both are JPEG files, image/jpeg. The download ends in .jpg.
- **Pixels**: the width and height are the same. Nothing is cropped or scaled.
- **Encoder and quality**: the copy is written by MozJPEG at quality 82. Quality numbers aren't a shared scale, so 82 here and 82 in another program can give different results.
- **Layout**: the copy is a progressive JPEG with optimized Huffman tables.
- **Metadata**: the copy carries no EXIF, ICC profile or XMP. Camera settings, the date taken and GPS location stay only in your original.
- **Orientation**: the page neither applies nor saves the EXIF orientation tag, so a photo that relies on it to look upright may come out turned.
- **Size**: if the copy isn't smaller than your file, the page returns your file instead.

Every JPEG save is lossy, including this one. Compress from the best copy you have, once, rather than squeezing the same file again and again.

### Other ways to compress a JPG

- **Preview (Mac):** with the image open, choose File > Export, set the Format pop-up to JPEG, change the quality, then press Save.
- **Photos (Mac):** select the photos and choose File > Export > Export Photos. Pick JPEG from the Photo Kind menu, open the options with the arrow beside it to set JPEG Quality and Size, then click Export.
- **GIMP (Windows, Mac and Linux):** open the image and use File > Export As (Shift+Ctrl+E); in the JPEG options, set Quality below its default of 85 and export.

### Problems with JPG files

- **Still over an upload limit**: this page changes only the quality. Shrink the photo's pixel dimensions in an editor, then compress the smaller copy.
- **The same file came back**: the quality 82 encode wasn't smaller than your file, so there was nothing to save.
- **Text and sharp lines look smudged**: JPEG is lossy. Keep screenshots, logos and diagrams as PNG and shrink them with the [PNG compressor](/compress-png/).
- **The location and camera details are gone**: EXIF is not written to the copy. Keep your original when you need them.
- **Colors look different**: no ICC profile goes into the smaller copy. Keep the original when color accuracy matters.
- **The photo comes out sideways**: the orientation tag is dropped. Rotate the picture in an editor before you compress it.
- **Blocky patches show up after repeats**: every save costs more detail. Start again from the original instead of recompressing a compressed copy.

faqs.question: How do I convert a CR2 to JPG?
faqs.answer: Pick your CR2 files above. Each one is decoded in your browser by ImageMagick, which uses LibRaw for raw files, and the JPG downloads once it is ready. The CR2 itself stays untouched.

faqs.question: How do I convert CR2 to JPG in bulk?
faqs.answer: Pick every CR2 from the card in one go and the page works through them in order. Each JPG is saved under its CR2's name and nothing is zipped, so expect one download per photo.

faqs.question: Can I convert CR2 to JPG without losing quality?
faqs.answer: Not entirely. JPEG is lossy, and the page gives no quality setting. Keep the CR2 as your master and treat the JPG as the copy you share.

faqs.question: Can I change the brightness or color before it converts?

faqs.question: What does "The RAW file is damaged" mean?
faqs.answer: The decoder reported the CR2 as damaged or cut short. Copy it off the card a second time and convert that fresh copy.

faqs.question: Why is the JPG not the same as the preview on my camera?
faqs.answer: Software must convert the sensor data of a raw file into color and tone, and each program decides how. A developed JPG can therefore differ in brightness and color from what your camera showed. To steer the look, develop the file in darktable and export from there.

faqs.question: Which Canon cameras does it support?
faqs.answer: A recognized .cr2 ending does not guarantee that a program supports the camera that made the file. The decoder this page uses is LibRaw, which lists the Canon cameras it supports. CR3 files from newer Canon bodies are a different format; the site has a separate [CR3 to JPG converter](/cr3-to-jpg/) for them.

faqs.question: Can I open a CR2 without converting it?
faqs.answer: Yes, with Canon Digital Photo Professional, darktable or Adobe Camera Raw, provided your camera model is supported. Adobe lists a minimum plug-in version for each camera.

faqs.question: Is there a PNG option for my CR2?
faqs.answer: Yes. The site has a [CR2 to PNG converter](/cr2-to-png/) if you want PNG instead of JPG.

faqs.question: Is my CR2 uploaded to a server?
faqs.answer: No. The work is done by ImageMagick compiled to WebAssembly inside this page, so no server gets your CR2. The raw file is not modified, and a JPG is saved as a new file.

guide.title: About CR2 files
guide.markdown:
### What is a CR2 file?

CR2 is Canon's raw image format, the one many EOS cameras wrote from the mid-2000s until CR3 replaced it. Raw means the file holds the sensor's measurements instead of a finished picture. Software has to process them, choosing white balance, tone and color, before they look like a photograph.

A CR2 is built on TIFF, and it carries an embedded JPEG preview next to the sensor data. Canon's own Digital Photo Professional lists .CR2 among the raw extensions it reads.

You usually meet a CR2 when you copy a shoot off the memory card of a Canon camera and find that your phone, an email program or an upload form will not show it. A JPG fixes that.

Raw files exist so you can make those choices after the shot. The catch is that CR2 is a proprietary camera format. A program that recognizes the extension may still not support the camera that made the file.

### Programs that open CR2 files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** darktable lists CR2 as an import extension, and decoding depends on camera support.
- **Windows and Mac:** Canon Digital Photo Professional is Canon's own program and reads CR2 files from the cameras it lists. Adobe Camera Raw supports Canon cameras by model and by minimum plug-in version, so check Adobe's supported-camera list.
- **Linux:** LibRaw's dcraw_emu is a command-line raw developer; LibRaw lists the Canon cameras it supports.
- **Web and mobile:** browsers do not display CR2. This page decodes it with ImageMagick inside the page.

### CR2 and JPG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .cr2 is Canon-specific; .jpg or .jpeg is image/jpeg.
- **What is stored**: a CR2 holds unprocessed sensor data and a small preview. A JPG holds a processed picture.
- **Compression**: JPEG is lossy. The raw data in a CR2 is not a rendered picture at all.
- **Editing room**: raw leaves white balance and tone adjustments open until you process it. A JPG has them baked in.
- **Color depth**: JPEG stores 8 bits per channel, and this page works at 8 bits.
- **Reach**: all major browsers show JPEG, and it comes straight out of most digital cameras and scanners. CR2 needs a decoder that knows your camera.

Its name comes from a committee, the Joint Photographic Experts Group; the ISO/IEC 10918-1 standard dates from 1994. Most programs expose quality as a number from 0 to 100, yet equal numbers in two programs can look different.

The step from CR2 to JPG is a processing step as well as a format change. After it, you have one picture, not a file you can re-develop. For a result you control, develop the CR2 in a raw editor first, then export the JPG from there. If you only need a quick copy to share or to check focus, the converter on this page is enough.

### Other ways to convert CR2 to JPG

- **darktable (Windows, Mac, Linux):** import the CR2 and select it. In the export module, target storage is set to file on disk; then JPEG is chosen as the format, and you press export. The module has a quality setting for JPEG, which defaults to 95.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick cr2:portrait.cr2 portrait.jpg`. ImageMagick's format list says CR2 needs the explicit `cr2:` specifier before the file name. In a test with a sample CR2 this wrote a JPG.

### Problems with CR2 files

- **The program says it cannot read the file**: the extension is recognized but your camera model is not. Update the program, or convert with a decoder that lists the camera.
- **Brightness and color differ from your camera**: the camera, this page and your editor each turn the sensor data into a picture in their own way, so the results will not match.
- **"The RAW file is damaged." or "ends before its picture does"**: the decoder reports the file as cut off or corrupt. Copy it from the card again.
- **Too large to convert**: roughly 537 megapixels is the ceiling; above it you see a message that the picture is too big for this page.
- **You worry the CR2 will not open in future**: it is a proprietary camera format, so long-term access depends on programs keeping support for it. Hold on to the original file.
- **The JPG looks flat**: this page has no tone or color controls. Use darktable to adjust the picture and export your own JPG.

faqs.question: How does CSV combining work?
faqs.answer: Our CSV combiner merges multiple CSV files by aligning columns with matching headers. It intelligently handles different column orders and missing columns, creating a unified dataset.

faqs.question: What happens to duplicate headers?
faqs.answer: When files have the same column headers, the data is merged vertically (rows are appended). If headers differ, new columns are created and empty cells are filled with blank values for missing data.

faqs.question: Is there a file size limit?
faqs.answer: You can combine CSV files up to 50MB each. The tool processes files locally in your browser, so performance depends on your device's memory.

faqs.question: Can I combine files with different encodings?
faqs.answer: Yes, the tool automatically detects and handles various text encodings including UTF-8, UTF-16, and ASCII, ensuring proper character display in the merged file.

faqs.question: How are different delimiters handled?
faqs.answer: The combiner auto-detects delimiters (comma, semicolon, tab, pipe) in each file and standardizes them to your chosen output format.

guide.title: About DDS files
guide.markdown:
### What is a DDS file?

DirectDraw Surface, or DDS, is Microsoft's texture-file format, which came out of DirectX. Games use it for textures that a graphics card can load without further work. Inside, a DDS may store plain pixels or compressed texture data, usually in the DXT or BC block formats. Its listed uses are game textures, GPU-ready assets, and cubemaps and volume textures.

The file can also carry a mipmap chain next to its largest surface, plus cube maps and volume textures. Direct3D 10 and 11 added a second header, the DX10 extension, which covers texture arrays and pixel formats that the original header structure cannot express. An ordinary DDS is at least 128 bytes long because of its header, and 148 bytes when the DX10 extension is present.

### Programs that open DDS files

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- GIMP has handled DDS in its core plug-ins since version 2.10.10, so it loads and exports DDS out of the box.
- ImageMagick reads and writes DDS, and its documentation covers DXT compression and mipmap options.

### DDS and PNG compared

- **Extensions**: .dds and .png. PNG's media type is image/png.
- **Compression**: a DDS commonly keeps GPU block data in the DXT/BC formats. PNG always compresses losslessly.
- **Mipmaps and extras**: DDS can hold mipmaps, cube maps and volumes. A PNG holds a single picture.
- **Alpha**: both can carry an alpha channel.
- **Color depth**: PNG stores between 1 and 16 bits per sample.
- **Support**: every major browser displays PNG.
- **Extension headers**: the DX10 header of a DDS describes formats the original header cannot, and a PNG has no counterpart for it.
- **Typical use**: DDS holds game textures and other assets that are ready for a GPU. PNG is used for screenshots, interface graphics and logos.

This converter swaps a texture file for an ordinary picture. Detail that DXT compression dropped when the texture was made does not come back.

### Other ways to convert DDS to PNG

- **Microsoft DirectXTex (texconv):** run `texconv -ft png input.dds`. The -ft option sets the output type, which can also be bmp, jpg, tga, hdr, tif, wdp or ppm, and `-o` names the output directory. The `--ignore-mips` flag loads only the top mip level, which the texconv page suggests for malformed files that are missing data.
- **GIMP:** load the DDS and pick File > Export As, then enter the name texture.png. GIMP loads DDS from version 2.10.10 on, and clicking Export opens the options for the PNG format.
- **ImageMagick:** run `magick input.dds output.png`. The format list marks DDS as readable and writable, with DXT and mipmap options, and notes that PNG needs libpng.

### Problems with DDS files

- **The file won't open in an editor**: some DDS readers reject the DX10 header extension, while legacy RGB or DXT1 to DXT5 headers work in more tools. Re-export the texture with one of those.
- **The file is cut short**: a truncated header makes a DDS invalid, because the header alone needs 128 bytes, or 148 with the DX10 extension. Copy the file again from its source.
- **Only one picture comes out**: a DDS asset can hold a mipmap chain beside its largest surface, and cube maps and volume textures hold several faces or slices. A PNG holds a single image, so it cannot carry all of them.
- **A garbled picture**: wrong pitch information, the number of bytes in a row, corrupts how a reader splits scan lines. Microsoft recommends computing the pitch for the stored pixel format.
- **A header that is nonstandard**: texconv's `--permissive` option lets it load some malformed and variant headers that it would otherwise refuse.
- **Older DXTn files with short mip blocks**: the smallest mip levels of some old files are slightly short. texconv's `--bad-tails` option copies the 4x4 data into those levels, which avoids corrupted data though it is not a full recompute.
- **A BC texture whose top level isn't a multiple of 4**: Direct3D requires a multiple of 4, and texconv's `--fix-bc-4x4` option resizes such images, after which the mipmaps need regenerating.
- **Legacy 24-bit files**: texconv has a `-dword` option for old DWORD-aligned files, which are typically 24 bits per pixel.
- **Typeless pixel formats**: texconv's page warns that typeless formats will generally fail most operations, with `-tu` and `-tf` available to treat them as UNORM or float.

guide.title: About DNG files
guide.markdown:
### What is a DNG file?

DNG, Digital Negative, is a format Adobe published for camera raw data, with the first specification dating to September 2004. It extends the TIFF family with the tags a program needs to interpret a raw photograph. Raw means the file holds what the sensor measured, not a finished picture, so software has to develop it before you see a photo.

A DNG can come straight from a camera or phone that writes the format. It can also be made with Adobe's DNG Converter, which translates supported proprietary raw files into DNG. Inside, it may hold the mosaic of sensor data or an already demosaiced, linear version, and it can use lossless JPEG compression. Exif metadata can ride along.

You usually meet a DNG when you copy photos from a phone's pro camera mode or from an editing catalog, and find that an upload form, a chat app or a website will not show it. A JPG fixes that, and it opens almost anywhere. The DNG stays the better starting point if you may want a different color treatment later, so keep it after you convert.

### Programs that open DNG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** darktable accepts the .dng extension on import, though its decoding limits still apply. ImageMagick reads DNG too, and the dng: prefix names the format when it has to be explicit.
- **Windows and Mac:** DNG is handled by Adobe Camera Raw inside compatible Adobe applications, part of Adobe's raw workflow.

### DNG and JPG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: Digital Negative files end in .dng. JPEG files end in .jpg or .jpeg and use image/jpeg.
- **Contents**: a DNG holds raw sensor data or a linear version, plus the tags to interpret it. A JPG holds a finished picture.
- **Compression**: a DNG can use lossless JPEG compression. A JPG is always lossy.
- **Editing room**: raw leaves white balance, exposure and tone open for later. A JPG has them baked in.
- **Metadata**: a DNG can hold Exif metadata, but this page does not promise that tags carry over to the JPG.
- **Support**: JPG opens everywhere. A DNG needs a raw-aware program.

On this page the raw data goes through ImageMagick with no controls offered, and the result is saved as a JPG named after your DNG. You get a normal photo, but you cannot change white balance, exposure or noise handling before it is written. If the look matters, develop in a raw editor and export from there, then use the JPG for sharing. The page takes several files at once and hands you each JPG separately.

### Other ways to convert DNG to JPG

- **darktable (Windows, Mac, Linux):** highlight the DNG in the filmstrip, find the export module, switch target storage to file on disk, pick JPEG for the format and press start export. The module offers a quality setting. Cameras with non-Bayer sensors are a known gap, with an exception for Fujifilm X-Trans.

### Problems with DNG files

- **A viewer shows nothing or a tiny picture**: ordinary viewers do not develop raw data. Open the DNG in a raw editor, or convert it here.
- **The page says the compression can't be decoded**: the message points at Nikon's newer raw compression, JPEG XL inside a DNG, and GoPro files. Use a raw editor for these.
- **The page says the RAW file is damaged or ends early**: the copy may be incomplete. Copy it from the source again, whether that is a card, a phone or a cloud folder.
- **The JPG looks flatter than expected**: the page lets you tune nothing, so adjust tone and color in an editor afterward.
- **A linear DNG behaves differently**: it is already demosaiced, so it is not interchangeable with untouched sensor-mosaic data. Check how it was made.
- **A huge picture is refused**: anything over about 537 megapixels is too large for the converter here.
- **Converting to DNG did not help a program read it**: DNG does not guarantee that every reader supports the sensor pattern inside. darktable documents limits for non-Bayer sensors, so check your camera in the program you use.
- **Renaming does nothing**: giving a DNG a .jpg ending leaves raw data inside, and no viewer will treat it as a photo.
- **A proprietary raw file will not open**: Adobe suggests verifying that DNG Converter lists the camera before you rely on it.

infoArticle.title: About 123Movies Video downloads
infoArticle.markdown:
A movie found on a 123Movies mirror tonight could be gone by tomorrow. Domains change, links break, and content you planned to watch later vanishes. Save it as an MP4 file on your own computer and watch it whenever you want.

This browser extension works across 123Movies mirrors and domain variants. Press play, click the extension icon, pick your quality, and the video downloads straight to your device. It handles full-length films reliably, with smart retry logic that keeps long downloads on track even when your connection drops. No extra software, no command line, no screen recording workarounds.

Everything happens inside your browser. The video never touches a third-party server, so what you download stays between you and your hard drive. Three free downloads are included so you can try it before committing.

faqs.question: How do I download a video from 123Movies?
faqs.answer: Open a supported 123Movies mirror, start playing the video, click the extension icon, choose your preferred quality, and start the download. The extension detects the active stream and saves the finished video as an MP4 file.

faqs.question: Do I need to press play before detection works?
faqs.answer: Yes. The extension detects the stream after playback starts. If no video appears in the popup, press play first, wait for the stream to load, and then open the extension again.

faqs.question: What quality options are available?
faqs.answer: When the source provides multiple renditions, the extension can show a manual quality selector alongside an automatic best-quality option. Typical stream variants depend on the mirror and may include resolutions such as 720p, 480p, or 360p.

faqs.question: What format are the downloaded videos?
faqs.answer: Videos are saved as standard MP4 files. HLS streams are stitched and converted to MP4 in-browser, while direct MP4 sources are saved directly when available.

faqs.question: Does it support multiple downloads at once?
faqs.answer: No. This downloader is optimized for one video at a time so the active stream can be processed cleanly. Start the next download after the current file finishes.

faqs.question: Will this work on every 123Movies domain?
faqs.answer: It is designed for 123Movies mirrors and domain variants, including domains containing "123movies" or "123-movies". Support depends on the mirror exposing a compatible video stream and not using DRM.

faqs.question: Why is the extension requesting these permissions?
faqs.answer: 123Movies mirrors often use redirects, embedded players, and hidden stream manifests. Permissions like tabs, webRequest, scripting, and downloads let the extension detect the active video, resolve the real media source, track progress, and save the MP4 locally.

faqs.question: Which browsers are supported?
faqs.answer: Desktop builds are available for Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Brave, Opera, Whale, and Yandex on Windows, macOS, and Linux. Safari and mobile browsers are not supported.

faqs.question: Why is my video not being detected?
faqs.answer: Press play first and give the stream a moment to initialize. If the mirror still does not appear, refresh the page and try again. Detection also fails on unsupported or DRM-protected streams.

faqs.question: Is there a free trial?
faqs.answer: Yes. You get 3 free trial downloads after signing in with your email. After that, the product uses a paid subscription for unlimited downloads.

faqs.question: Is my data private?
faqs.answer: Yes. Video processing happens locally in your browser. Authentication uses secure OTP email verification, and the extension does not upload video files to external servers.

faqs.question: Is this legal?
faqs.answer:
DISCLAIMER: We are not attorneys and do not offer legal advice. Laws vary by country and platform. For any legal question please consult a qualified legal professional.
We give you full control over download speeds because we believe users should decide how they use their software.
That said, here are a few widely accepted best practices for safe, responsible downloading:
Only download content you created, own, or have explicit permission from the rights holder to access.
Protect your personal data by respecting platform rules and rate limits with reasonable download speeds to avoid automated abuse systems putting your account at risk.
Protect your privacy by using a reputable VPN for IP protection before initiating downloads — this is the VPN we recommend & use .

infoArticle.title: About DreamCam downloads
infoArticle.markdown:
DreamCam does not offer any way to download content. Live shows are here one moment and gone the next, with no option to save them. DreamCam Downloader lets you capture live public streams and save available recordings so you have permanent copies.

Open a live room or recording page on DreamCam, pick your quality, and either record a live stream or download a saved video. Live capture gives you start and stop controls so you decide exactly what to keep.

The extension is built specifically for DreamCam, finding streams where generic tools fail. Files save automatically to a DREAMCAM folder on your computer. Everything happens locally in your browser with nothing sent elsewhere. Start with 3 free downloads.

faqs.question: How do I record a live stream from DreamCam?
faqs.answer: Open a public live model page on DreamCam, let the player load, then use the in-player button, extension popup, or the "Download DreamCam Stream" context-menu action. Choose a quality and press Start. When you want to end the capture, press Stop and the extension finalizes the MP4.

faqs.question: Can it download recordings too?
faqs.answer: Yes. On supported video pages the extension switches to a standard download flow, detects the available recording formats, and saves the selected video as MP4 without using the live-capture stop step.

faqs.question: What quality options are available?
faqs.answer: The extension reads the HLS master playlist and related DreamCam APIs to list the renditions the current stream or recording exposes. That usually means multiple resolutions and can include frame-rate differences where available.

faqs.question: Does it support VR metadata?
faqs.answer: Yes. If DreamCam exposes VR camera settings, the extension detects stereo packing, frame format, and viewing-angle details so the saved workflow can preserve the context needed for VR playback.

faqs.question: What format are the downloads?
faqs.answer: All saved media is written as MP4. Direct file sources can download immediately, while HLS-based sources are captured or stitched into MP4 locally before the job completes.

faqs.question: Where are files saved?
faqs.answer: Completed downloads are written automatically to a DREAMCAM folder inside your browser's default Downloads directory.

faqs.question: Does it work for private shows?
faqs.answer: No. The extension is intended for content your current session can already access in a public or otherwise available workflow. It does not bypass private or inaccessible shows.

faqs.question: Can I run multiple captures at once?
faqs.answer: No. This product is optimized for one active capture or download at a time so live polling, segment handling, and MP4 assembly remain stable.

faqs.question: Which browsers are supported?
faqs.answer: Desktop builds support Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Brave, Opera, Whale, and Yandex on Windows, macOS, and Linux. Safari and mobile browsers are not supported.

faqs.question: How does the free trial work?
faqs.answer: After secure email OTP sign-in, you get 3 free downloads on the current device. Unlimited downloads require the monthly subscription configured for this product.

faqs.question: Why is no stream showing up?
faqs.answer: Make sure the model is publicly live and let playback start before checking the quality list. If the model is offline, the room is private, or the page has not fully loaded, the extension may not have enough stream data yet. Refresh and retry if needed.

faqs.question: Is my data private?
faqs.answer: Yes. Stream detection, capture, and MP4 generation happen locally in your browser. Remote requests are limited to activation, update checks, and the original page or API calls needed to resolve the media you already access.

infoArticle.title: About FanslyLive downloads
infoArticle.markdown:
Fansly live streams are ephemeral by design. Once a broadcast ends, the content often disappears unless the creator explicitly saves a replay. If you missed the window or your connection dropped mid-stream, that content is gone. Fansly Live Downloader captures authorized live broadcasts as they happen, writing standard MP4 files to your local storage so you retain a permanent copy of streams you were entitled to watch.

The workflow is straightforward. Open a Fansly live stream page in your browser while logged in to your subscriber account. The extension detects the active broadcast and presents a record button in the toolbar popup. Press record and the incoming stream data is captured frame by frame and assembled into an MP4 container on your hard drive. Audio and video stay synchronized throughout, even when the streamer switches between camera angles or adjusts their broadcast settings mid-session.

Recording happens entirely within your browser. No data is routed through external relay servers, no temporary copies are staged in the cloud, and no metadata about your viewing habits leaves your machine. The extension communicates with Fansly to receive the stream and with a license server for activation — nothing else.

You can pause and resume recording during a single broadcast if you only want specific segments. Each saved file is automatically named with the creator handle and timestamp, making it easy to organize a growing archive without manual renaming. When the stream ends naturally or you stop recording, the file is finalized and immediately playable in any standard video player.

Compatible with Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Brave, and Opera across Windows, macOS, and Linux. Three free recording sessions are included so you can verify quality and compatibility before purchasing a full license.

infoArticle.title: About StripchatVR downloads
infoArticle.markdown:
Virtual reality cam content on Stripchat is designed for real-time consumption. Once a VR session ends, viewers lose access unless the performer posts a replay. This downloader bridges that gap by saving VR cam recordings to your local storage as standard video files, ready for offline playback in any VR headset or desktop player that supports side-by-side or equirectangular formats.

When you visit a Stripchat VR recording page while logged in, the extension identifies the VR stream endpoints and presents the available quality options in a clean toolbar popup. Select your preferred resolution, hit download, and the file streams directly from Stripchat servers to your hard drive. There is no cloud relay, no temporary staging on third-party infrastructure, and no intermediary that ever touches your data.

The extension preserves the spatial metadata embedded in VR recordings so that headsets like Meta Quest, Valve Index, and PSVR interpret the projection correctly on playback. You get the same immersive field of view offline that you experienced during the live session. Standard 2D monitors will display the file as a flat side-by-side frame, which is normal for VR video files.

File naming is automated using the performer handle and recording timestamp, which keeps your VR library organized without manual effort. A built-in duplicate checker prevents re-downloading files you have already saved, and pause-resume support means large VR files, often several gigabytes, can survive connection interruptions without starting over.

No analytics, no usage tracking, no external callbacks. The extension communicates with Stripchat for video data and a license server for activation. Everything else stays on your machine. Compatible with Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Brave, and Opera on Windows, macOS, and Linux. Three free downloads let you verify headset compatibility before committing to a license.

xHamsterLive cam sessions are transient. Performers go live, interact with their audience, and when the session ends the content is typically gone unless a recorded replay surfaces later. This downloader lets you capture live cam sessions in real time, writing the incoming stream directly to an MP4 file on your local device so you maintain a permanent offline copy of broadcasts you were authorized to view.

Open any active xHamsterLive cam room in your browser while logged in to your account. The extension detects the live stream and adds a capture button to the toolbar popup. Click it, and the broadcast is recorded locally as it plays. The extension intercepts the stream data at the browser level and writes it to disk without re-encoding, preserving the original quality and keeping CPU usage low.

If a session runs for hours, the extension handles it gracefully. Automatic segment stitching assembles long recordings into a single continuous file, and a heartbeat monitor watches for stream interruptions. If the feed drops temporarily and resumes, the recorder picks up again without creating a separate file. You end up with one clean MP4 per session.

Every file is named automatically using the performer's handle and the session start time. This convention makes it simple to browse a large collection weeks or months later without trying to remember which file is which. Duplicate detection prevents you from accidentally re-recording a session you have already saved.

The entire process is local. No stream data is uploaded to external servers, no recording logs are transmitted, and no analytics are collected. The extension talks to xHamsterLive for stream access and to a license server for activation. That is the complete list of network destinations. Works on Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Brave, and Opera across Windows, macOS, and Linux. Three free capture sessions are included.

infoArticle.title: About Galaxyporn video downloads
infoArticle.markdown:
GalaxyPorn operates as an aggregator-style platform where video playback often travels across multiple third-party providers. The video you see on a GalaxyPorn page may actually be served from a completely different host, making it difficult to save with standard browser tools or generic downloaders.

This extension is built around that reality. Instead of assuming the page host tells the whole story, Galaxyporn Downloader is framed to work with GalaxyPorn pages and the wider helper-host constellation behind playback. It uses an in-player button and shared media detection patterns so you can save videos without manually hunting for the source URL across multiple domains.

**How it works**

- Install the extension from the latest release.
- Open GalaxyPorn and go to a supported video page.
- Start playback so the extension can detect the media.
- Open the popup or use the on-page controls.
- Choose the quality option you want.
- Start the download and wait for the MP4 export to finish.
- Save the final file locally.

**Supported formats**

- Input: Video streams detected on GalaxyPorn pages and associated helper hosts using standard metadata and media tag patterns
- Output: MP4
- Saved files use MP4 so they are easier to replay on standard media players, move between devices, or archive locally.

**Troubleshooting**

- The player button does not appear on the video page Make sure the video player has fully loaded and playback has started. The button attaches to the configured player wrapper, which may take a moment to render.
- The download does not start after clicking the button Check that you have an active internet connection and that the video source is still accessible. Some helper hosts may have expired or rotated their stream URLs.
- The extension cannot detect any media on the page Not all GalaxyPorn pages may expose detectable media through the standard patterns. Try refreshing the page or starting playback again to trigger host resolution.
- I see an error about permissions The extension requires permissions for downloads, active tab access, and storage. Make sure you have granted these permissions during installation.
- The downloaded file will not play on my device Ensure you have a media player that supports MP4 files. If the file is corrupted, try downloading again from a different quality option.

**Notes**

- Only download content you own or have explicit permission to save
- An internet connection is required for downloads
- GalaxyPorn playback may depend on helper hosts outside the main page domain
- The current profile still needs real extraction review before full release readiness

faqs.question: How do I convert FLAC to WAV?
faqs.answer: Select your FLAC file here, let it finish and save the WAV. If you add several files, they run in sequence and every one downloads as its own WAV.

faqs.question: Does converting FLAC to WAV lose quality?

faqs.question: What happens to my 24-bit FLAC?
faqs.answer: It comes out as a 16-bit WAV. FLAC supports sample depths from 4 to 32 bits, but this page always writes 16-bit PCM, so the extra precision is lost. For a 24-bit WAV use FFmpeg with pcm_s24le.

faqs.question: Why did my WAV come out so much larger than the FLAC?
faqs.answer: WAV normally stores uncompressed PCM, while FLAC packs the same samples more tightly without discarding any. FLAC usually lands near half the uncompressed size, so plan for a WAV about twice as large.

faqs.question: Is there a file size limit for the WAV?
faqs.answer: The page itself caps nothing, but the original WAV layout stops at 4 GB, and very large recordings need RF64 instead of the RIFF size fields. The work happens locally, so a long file simply takes longer to process.

faqs.question: Will the album art and tags carry over?
faqs.answer: By default FFmpeg carries a file's global tags (title, artist, album and so on) over when the output format can store them. FLAC keeps tags as Vorbis comments and can hold pictures, while WAV stores information in INFO chunks or Broadcast WAVE extensions. Keep the FLAC as the file with your full tags and album art.

faqs.question: Can I choose the sample rate or channel count?
faqs.answer: No. The page sets neither, so the WAV follows FFmpeg's defaults for your file. If you need a specific rate or channel layout, use Audacity or FFmpeg.

faqs.question: Why would I convert FLAC to WAV at all?
faqs.answer: Some programs accept WAV but not FLAC. WAV is also used for audio recording and editing, professional sound production and as a source file before compression. Audacity and VLC open FLAC directly, so check before you convert.

faqs.question: Can converting a lossy file to FLAC and then WAV bring back quality?
faqs.answer: No. Lossy audio that went into a FLAC stays lossy, because samples removed earlier can't be recreated, and the WAV made from it inherits that.

faqs.question: Why does the converter fail with an FFmpeg error?
faqs.answer: FFmpeg could not read the file as audio, for example because it is not a FLAC at all. The page then shows an FFmpeg failure message.

guide.title: About FLAC files
guide.markdown:
### What is a FLAC file?

FLAC stands for Free Lossless Audio Codec. It compresses integer PCM audio without discarding any sample information, so decoding gives back exactly what went in. December 2024 brought RFC 9639, which standardized the format description. The specification is open, and the reference implementation is open source.

A FLAC stream holds one to eight channels at sample depths of 4 to 32 bits. Metadata blocks can carry seek points, pictures such as album art, and Vorbis comments for tags, and the media type is audio/flac. It suits music archiving, audiophile listening and lossless CD backups, since the files are about half the size of uncompressed audio and lose nothing.

### Programs that open FLAC files

**Windows, macOS and Linux**

- foobar2000 and Apple Music: also open FLAC.
- VLC media player: FLAC is on its list of input formats.
- Audacity: reads FLAC on its own; the optional FFmpeg library isn't needed.
- ffplay: the FFmpeg player, which plays FLAC through FFmpeg decoders.

**Web**

- Firefox decodes FLAC, and Chrome lists FLAC decoding in Mozilla's browser support comparison.

**Mobile**

- On Android and iOS, VLC opens FLAC files as they are, without converting.

### FLAC and WAV compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .flac and audio/flac; .wav, with audio/wav and audio/x-wav in common use.
- **What they are**: FLAC is a codec with its own stream format. WAV is a RIFF-based wrapper for sound that can carry several encodings.
- **Fidelity**: both keep every sample. FLAC compresses without discarding any, and the linear PCM in a WAV is exact, so neither is a lossy format.
- **Compression**: FLAC compresses. WAV usually holds linear PCM, which is uncompressed, although compressed encodings can appear too.
- **Bit depth**: FLAC covers 4 to 32 bits. This converter writes 16-bit PCM.
- **Metadata**: FLAC uses Vorbis comments and can embed pictures. WAV uses INFO chunks, and Broadcast WAVE adds production and preservation metadata.
- **Size**: FLAC typically halves the size of the audio. WAV has a 4 GB file size limit, and very large recordings need RF64.
- **Use**: for digital audio collections the Library of Congress recommends WAVE.

WAV opens in Audacity, VLC media player, Windows Media Player and any web browser, which is part of why it works as a common handoff format. The conversion changes the packing and fixes the depth at 16 bits: FFmpeg in your browser decodes the FLAC and writes 16-bit PCM into the WAV. A 16-bit source loses nothing, while a 24-bit source drops to 16 bits.

### Other ways to convert FLAC to WAV

- **flac command-line tool:** run `flac -d album-track.flac`. Decoding creates a WAV by default. The flac tool reads FLAC natively.
- **Audacity (Windows, Mac, Linux):** open the FLAC, choose File > Export Audio, pick WAV and choose the PCM encoding you need. The Encoding menu defaults to Signed 16-bit PCM.
- **FFmpeg (command line):** run `ffmpeg -i album-track.flac -c:a pcm_s24le album-track.wav` for 24-bit PCM output. Pick the encoding that matches your source.

### Problems with FLAC files

- **A device won't play it**: Android's documented native FLAC support covers mono or stereo and recommends 16-bit samples, which is less than the format allows. VLC for Android copes with more.
- **The file reports an error or skips**: FLAC checks each frame, so damage shows up as a checksum failure. Lossless coding can't protect against a bad disk or a broken download, so copy the file again.
- **The music sounds the same as an MP3**: if the FLAC was made from a lossy file, the removed samples are gone for good. A FLAC is only as good as what went into it.
- **A program needs WAV**: convert here, or in Audacity if you need to choose the encoding.
- **The WAV is too big to store or send**: WAV is large but exact. Keep the FLAC for storage, which is about half the size, and make the WAV only when a program needs it.
- **The WAV stops at 4 GB**: that is the original limit of the format. For a recording that long, use a tool that writes RF64.
- **Some tags are missing in the WAV**: A WAV has no Vorbis comments, so some fields may have nowhere to go. Keep the FLAC, and tag the WAV in your editor.

faqs.question: What bitrate is the MP3?
faqs.answer: 192 kbps is what the page asks the LAME encoder for. LAME writes at most 160 kbps for FLV sound at 16 to 24 kHz and at most 64 kbps for 8 to 12 kHz, so a low-quality source gets a lower rate. There is no setting to change it on this page.

faqs.question: Do I need Flash Player to convert an FLV?

faqs.question: Why does my FLV to MP3 conversion fail?

faqs.question: Will the MP3 sound worse than the FLV?
faqs.answer: It can. The sound is decoded and compressed again as lossy MP3, even when the FLV's audio was already MP3. Keep the FLV if you want an archive copy.

faqs.question: Does the MP3 keep the video's title and other tags?
faqs.answer: The FLV's global tags, a title for example, are copied by FFmpeg into the MP3's ID3 fields where the MP3 can hold them. If the FLV carried none, the MP3 has none, and a tag editor can fill them in.

faqs.question: Can an FLV hold more than one audio track?
faqs.answer: An FLV holds at most one audio stream, so the format itself leaves nothing to choose between.

faqs.question: Is the video lost?
faqs.answer: Yes. An MP3 is audio only, so the video is not in the result. Convert FLV to MP4 instead if you want to keep the picture.

faqs.question: My FLV is large. Will it convert?
faqs.answer: Nothing on this page caps file size or sets a timeout, so a big FLV just keeps converting until your device finishes. Keep the tab open until the MP3 appears.

faqs.question: Can I convert several FLV files into MP3 together?
faqs.answer: Yes, queue as many as you like. Every FLV yields its own MP3 download; nothing is zipped or merged.

guide.title: About FLV and MP3
guide.markdown:
### What is an FLV file?

Flash Video, or FLV, is a container format created by Macromedia and later Adobe for delivering video through Flash Player. A single FLV carries no more than one video stream plus one audio stream. Its video is Sorenson or On2 VP6, and its sound may be MP3, PCM or ADPCM. A Flash SWF can point at a standalone FLV via ActionScript.

Support for Flash Player ended on December 31, 2020, which leaves FLV a legacy format. Older web video and archived Flash content is where you still meet it. The .flv ending does not identify a unique video codec, so two FLV files can need different decoders.

### Programs that open FLV files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** playback is covered by VLC media player, which lists FLV input plus Sorenson and VP6-family decoding, and by FFplay, which uses FFmpeg decoders for FLV.
- **Phones and tablets:** VLC exists for Android and for iOS, and both open files stored on the device.

Reinstalling Flash Player is not a way to play an old FLV, since it is discontinued.

### FLV and MP3 compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .flv for Flash Video; .mp3 for MP3.
- **What it holds**: an FLV is a video container with at most one video and one audio stream. An MP3 is audio only.
- **Compression**: sound inside an FLV may be MP3, PCM or ADPCM; the MP3 you get is lossy either way, with constant or variable bitrate possible.
- **Tags**: an MP3 stores metadata as ID3 tags.
- **Typical uses**: an MP3 suits music libraries and downloads, podcasts, and audio for portable players, which is why pulling the sound out of an old Flash clip often ends in this format.
- **Playback**: an MP3 plays on nearly every device and in any web browser, whereas an FLV needs a player with the right decoders.
- **Standards**: MP3 is MPEG-1/2 Audio Layer III, standardized by MPEG as ISO/IEC 11172-3, with major contributions from the Fraunhofer Society. It can use constant or variable bitrate.

Here is what happens when you convert, step by step. A worker in your browser runs FFmpeg as WebAssembly. It reads the FLV, ignores the video and has the LAME encoder write an MP3 with a requested rate of 192 kbps, which LAME lowers for sources with a low sample rate. Even when the FLV's sound was already MP3, it is decoded and encoded again, not copied. The file picker accepts .flv files only. The MP3 is named after your file, with the .mp3 extension, and your FLV is not changed.

Because of that second encode, the MP3 is not a bit-for-bit copy of the original sound. Several files can be queued together. They run one by one, and each finished MP3 downloads on its own, with no ZIP. If you only need the picture, use the [FLV to MP4 converter](/flv-to-mp4/) instead.

### Other ways to convert FLV to MP3

- **FFmpeg (command line):** the command is `ffmpeg -i archive.flv -vn -c:a libmp3lame -b:a 192k archive.mp3`. FFmpeg's documentation lists FLV among the formats it demuxes, and the FLV needs an audio stream.
- **GStreamer (command line):** use `gst-launch-1.0 filesrc location=archive.flv ! decodebin ! audioconvert ! audioresample ! lamemp3enc ! filesink location=archive.mp3`. Its flvdemux element demuxes FLV files, decodebin builds the decoding pipeline, and lamemp3enc writes the MP3.

### Problems with FLV files

- **The FLV does not play**: the extension does not identify the codec, and Sorenson or VP6 video needs a decoder. Try VLC, not a Flash Player reinstall.
- **No MP3 appears**: the FLV may have no audio track, in which case the converter shows an FFmpeg failure message.
- **The MP3 has no title or artist**: the FLV probably carried none, since FFmpeg copies the FLV's tags where MP3 has fields for them. Add them in a tag editor.
- **You need several audio tracks**: an FLV holds one audio stream, so a workflow with alternative audio tracks cannot keep that structure inside it.
- **The picture is gone and you want it**: an MP3 holds sound only. Go back to the FLV, or convert it to MP4.
- **A Flash page can't find its video**: a SWF can point to a separate FLV file, so move the FLV and the SWF together.

guide.title: About FLV files
guide.markdown:
### What is an FLV file?

FLV is a binary format created at Macromedia for delivering Flash video, later maintained by Adobe. One file can carry only a single video stream and a single audio stream. Video is usually Sorenson or On2 VP6, with MP3, PCM or ADPCM for sound. Flash movies in SWF files could pull in a separate FLV through ActionScript.

Flash Player support from Adobe stopped on December 31, 2020, so the browser plug-in that once played these files no longer exists. FLV lives on as older web video and as archived Flash content. Nothing in the extension tells you which codec is inside, and a program needs the matching decoder to show the picture.

### Programs that open FLV files

**Linux, Mac, Windows, Android and iOS**

- VLC media player: lists FLV (Flash) among its input formats, and its video decoders include Sorenson and On2 VP6.

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- mpv: opens FLV files.

### FLV and MP4 compared

- **Extensions and standards**: .flv for Flash Video, .mp4 for MPEG-4 Part 14, which is ISO/IEC 14496-14, first published in 2003. MP4's media types are video/mp4 and audio/mp4.
- **Streams**: an FLV is limited to one video and one audio stream. MP4 is a container for several codecs.
- **Codecs**: the usual FLV contents are Sorenson or VP6 video with MP3, PCM or ADPCM sound. This page writes H.264 and AAC, the common MP4 pair.
- **Streaming**: FLV was designed for streaming. The MP4 written here has its index placed first (the faststart option), so playback can begin before the download ends.
- **Players**: FLV opens in VLC and mpv today. Every major browser plays MP4, depending on the codecs inside.

Converting trades the original encoding for a format that current software expects. The video is decoded and encoded again, so quality drops a little, the audio becomes AAC at 96 kbps, and the settings are fixed: the ultrafast preset at CRF 32, shrunk to fit 1920 px and held to 30 fps at most.

### Other ways to convert FLV to MP4

- **FFmpeg stream copy (command line):** run `ffmpeg -i input.flv -c copy output.mp4`. This moves the streams into an MP4 without re-encoding them, so it is fast and loses nothing. It only works when MP4 can carry the source codecs: in a test, an FLV with H.264 video copied, but one with Sorenson video was refused.
- **FFmpeg transcoding (command line):** the command `ffmpeg -i input.flv -c:a aac -c:v libx264 output.mp4` encodes new H.264 and AAC streams, so both the picture and the sound are re-encoded.
- **HandBrake (desktop app):** open the FLV with the Open Source button, pick a preset such as Fast 1080p30, make sure the container is MP4, type a file name in Save As and press Start. HandBrake can open web videos in FLV and create MP4 files.

### Problems with FLV files

- **An old web page won't play its video**: the Flash player is retired. Convert the FLV itself; the MP4 doesn't bring back the page's Flash interface.
- **Stream copy fails or gives an MP4 that won't play**: the FLV's codecs aren't ones MP4 carries. Re-encode with this converter or the transcoding command.
- **The picture is smaller than the source**: a frame wider or taller than 1920 px is scaled down to fit, and an odd dimension loses a pixel. Keep the FLV if you need the exact original dimensions.
- **Motion looks less smooth**: a source above 30 fps is brought down to 30. Keep the FLV if the original timing matters. A clip at 25 or 30 fps is not affected.
- **The MP4 has no sound**: check whether the FLV had an audio stream. Play it in VLC first; a conversion can't add sound that was never there.
- **A SWF file won't play**: an old Flash movie (SWF) loaded its FLV through ActionScript. Converting the FLV does not rebuild that movie, so only the video comes across.
- **The FLV plays with no picture**: the video codec may be one your player has no decoder for. Try VLC, which decodes Sorenson and VP6.
- **A partial FLV gives a short MP4**: a download cut off midway has no data past that point, so the MP4 ends there too. Fetch the whole file again.

guide.title: About GIF and JPG files
guide.markdown:
### What is a GIF file?

GIF, the Graphics Interchange Format, was introduced by CompuServe in 1987. The 89a revision of July 1990 introduced extensions for clear pixels, frame delays, comments and application data. A GIF compresses images losslessly with LZW coding, and every image draws from a palette of 256 colors at most. Its registered media type is image/gif. Those extensions are what make animated GIFs possible.

A GIF is a stack of images, each held for its own delay in hundredths of a second, and that stack is the animation. Only one palette color can be flagged clear, which leaves every pixel either fully clear or fully opaque. That palette limit is why GIF suits flat-color graphics better than photographs. Browsers all show GIF. Colors come from color tables, and an image may use a table of its own instead of the one for the whole file, so the frames of one GIF can differ in color.

You meet GIFs as short looping animations, reaction images, stickers and simple graphics.

### Programs that open GIF files

**Mac, Linux and Windows**

- GIMP: an image editor named in the format reference.
- ImageMagick: a command-line tool whose supported formats include GIF.
- Mozilla Firefox: shows GIF in the browser.

**Mac**

- Preview: listed in the format reference for GIFs.

**Web and Mobile**

- Google Chrome displays GIF.

**Mobile**

- Safari displays GIF.

### GIF and JPG compared

- **Names**: .gif is image/gif, while .jpg or .jpeg is image/jpeg.
- **Compression**: GIF is lossless but limited to 256 colors per image. JPEG is lossy: it works on 8x8 pixel blocks, runs a discrete cosine transform on each and finishes with Huffman coding.
- **Color**: GIF is indexed color. JPEG keeps 8 bits for each color channel.
- **Transparency**: a GIF can mark one color as transparent. JPEG has no alpha channel.
- **Animation**: a GIF holds timed frames, one after another. A JPG is a single still.
- **Good for**: GIF for simple graphics and short loops. JPEG for photographs.
- **Metadata**: only pixels are written, so blocks such as EXIF, ICC and XMP are left behind, along with the GIF's comments.
- **Patents**: the LZW patents behind GIF expired in 2003 and 2004. JPEG's US patents expired in 2006.
- **Quality numbers**: GIF has none, since it is lossless. JPEG quality usually runs from 0 to 100, though one number gives different results in different programs.

On this page your browser decodes the GIF, then the canvas writes its first frame as a JPG at quality 0.85. Pixels that were see-through can't stay see-through, and an animation is cut to its first frame. EXIF, ICC and XMP metadata is dropped.

The download takes the GIF's name with .jpg in place of .gif. Several GIFs are handled in sequence, and every JPG lands in its own download.

### Other ways to convert GIF to JPG

- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux):** open the GIF and pick File > Export As. Select JPEG from the file-type list, press Export, and a JPEG settings dialog follows, with 85 as its default quality.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick 'input.gif[0]' output.jpg`. The [0] picks the first frame by number, and the quotes keep the brackets from being read by the shell.

Both give you control that this page does not, such as the quality setting.

### Problems with GIF files

- **Only one frame came out**: that is how a JPG works. Keep the GIF if you need the motion.
- **The see-through parts changed**: the GIF had transparency, which a JPG cannot hold. If you need it kept, convert to PNG instead with the [GIF to PNG converter](/gif-to-png/).
- **The first frame looks blank**: a GIF's first frame can be mostly see-through, and a JPG cannot keep see-through pixels, so check that the first frame is the one you want.
- **The timing is gone**: a GIF keeps a delay in hundredths of a second for each frame, and a JPG has nowhere to keep it.
- **Gradients look banded**: a GIF palette has at most 256 colors, and the JPG cannot restore the in-between shades.
- **A GIF will not open**: the file may be damaged, which the page reports as "Image decode failed." Re-download it from its source.
- **You need a different frame**: this page always takes the first. Use an editor that shows each frame separately.

guide.title: About GIF and WebM
guide.markdown:
### What is a GIF file?

GIF stands for Graphics Interchange Format. CompuServe introduced it in 1987. Every picture in a GIF is LZW-compressed and drawn from a palette limited to 256 colors. The GIF89a version added extensions for frame delays and for marking one palette color as transparent, which is what made short animations possible. Transparency is all or nothing: one palette color is declared transparent, and nothing can be partly see-through. The delay between pictures is set in hundredths of a second. Unisys' LZW licensing, which started in 1994, faded as patents lapsed, in the US in 2003 and a year later in Europe and Japan.

You meet GIFs as reaction clips, looping demos, stickers and small icons. The format stores pictures and timing, not sound. A GIF made from a movie clip lost its audio when it was made, and no converter can bring it back.

### Programs that open GIF files

- **Windows:** Photos opens GIFs.
- **Mac:** Preview opens GIFs.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP can export layered animations and still pictures, and an exported animated GIF can be set to loop forever. ImageMagick reads GIF.
- **Web and mobile:** every major browser displays GIFs; the ones named here are Chrome and Firefox on desktops and Safari and Chrome on phones.

### GIF and WebM compared

- **Extensions and types**: .gif is image/gif; .webm is video/webm.
- **What it is**: GIF is an image format that can animate. WebM is a video container based on Matroska, and it can hold VP8, VP9 or AV1 video.
- **Compression**: GIF compresses without loss, but only inside its 256-color palette. The WebM this page writes uses VP8 video.
- **Color**: the GIF palette limit is gone in the video, but colors that were already reduced in the GIF stay reduced.
- **Transparency**: GIF allows one fully transparent color. The WebM here is yuv420p, which has no alpha.
- **Sound**: GIF has none. The WebM from this page has none either, because the conversion switches audio off.
- **Looping**: the WebM from this page carries no loop setting, so a video repeats only if the page or player is told to.

FFmpeg decodes the GIF and passes its frames to the VP8 encoder (libvpx) at a fixed quality of CRF 40. The WebM follows the GIF's size and rate, but never exceeds 1920 px on its long side or 30 fps. Dimensions are rounded down to even values, which matters when a GIF is, say, 481 px wide. Interlaced frames, if a file has any, are deinterlaced first.

The file you get is a video, not an image. It opens in a player or sits in a video tag, and it has a play bar. To check it, play it in Chrome, Edge, Firefox or VLC media player; on a phone, try VLC for Android or VLC for iOS. Keep the GIF when the destination only accepts images.

### Other ways to convert GIF to WebM

- **FFmpeg (command line):** type `ffmpeg -i reaction.gif -c:v libvpx -pix_fmt yuv420p -an reaction.webm`. The command writes opaque VP8 video.
- **GStreamer (command line):** run `gst-launch-1.0 filesrc location=reaction.gif ! gifdec loop=force-no ! videoconvert ! vp8enc ! webmmux ! filesink location=reaction.webm`. It needs the gif, vpx and Matroska plug-ins.

### Problems with GIF files

- **The clip plays once and stops**: the converted file has no loop setting, so switch on repeat in your player or on the page's video tag.
- **Colors look speckled**: the GIF's 256-color palette causes dithering that no conversion removes. Go back to the original video if you still have it.
- **A site only accepts image uploads**: a form that wants .gif or an image type can reject video/webm. Keep the GIF there.
- **The picture has no transparent background**: a GIF marks one palette color as transparent, and the video here can't hold that. Place the clip on a matching background.
- **The GIF has no sound**: the format has no audio, so the WebM stays silent.
- **A very large GIF gets smaller**: a GIF wider or taller than 1920 px is shrunk to fit, and a smaller one is never scaled up.
- **A long GIF takes a while**: nothing on the page limits file size or running time, so a long GIF takes as long as your device needs.

guide.title: About GIF and WebP
guide.markdown:
### What is a GIF file?

GIF is the Graphics Interchange Format, introduced by CompuServe in 1987. A GIF compresses each picture with LZW and holds at most 256 colors per frame, drawn from a palette. It can hold several pictures with delays between them, which is how a GIF animates, and it can mark one palette color as fully transparent. GIF89a added the control blocks for delays and transparency.

GIFs are everywhere short, looping clips are shared: reaction images, stickers, instructions and small animated graphics. Because the palette is limited, a photograph in a GIF often shows dithering, and a smooth gradient shows bands. Converting the file does not undo that. The picture you start from is the palette picture, and WebP simply stores it in a different way.

### Programs that open GIF files

- **Windows:** Windows Photos opens GIF files. GIMP exports GIF as either a still picture or a multilayer animation.
- **Mac:** Preview opens GIF files, and GIMP exports GIF the same way.
- **Linux:** GIMP and ImageMagick, which reads GIF and can be scripted from the command line.
- **Web and mobile:** Chrome and Firefox show GIF on desktop websites; on phones, Chrome and Safari show it too.

To check the WebP you get from this page, open it in a current browser, since Chrome, Firefox and Safari all display WebP. GIMP has opened and saved WebP natively since 2.10, and Preview on macOS and Windows Photos open it as well.

### GIF and WebP compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .gif and image/gif; .webp and image/webp.
- **Compression**: GIF is lossless inside a 256-color limit. WebP offers a lossless mode and a lossy one, and the lossy one borrows its compression from the VP8 video codec.
- **Color**: WebP is not limited to a palette.
- **Transparency**: GIF has 1-bit transparency, a pixel either shows or does not. WebP has an alpha channel.
- **Animation**: both can animate. This page does not write an animated WebP.
- **Size limits**: WebP stops at 16,383 pixels per side, so anything larger cannot be stored as WebP.

The page decodes the first frame of the GIF with your browser's own image decoder and encodes it as a WebP with a browser canvas or ImageMagick, passing no quality setting. Metadata is not copied, and your original GIF is untouched. The picture passes through 8-bit RGBA, so a GIF's palette colors arrive as ordinary 8-bit pixels.

Google developed WebP and released it in 2010. Its lossy mode comes from the VP8 video codec; it also has a lossless mode, transparency and animation. It is used for web images with smaller files, for images that need transparency and for short animations.

A still WebP is useful when you want a web-friendly picture from the opening frame of an animation, for a thumbnail or a poster, for example. It keeps see-through pixels and sits comfortably on a page next to ordinary photos. If the motion matters, this page is the wrong tool; try one of the methods below.

### Other ways to convert GIF to WebP

- **gif2webp (Google):** run `gif2webp animation.gif -o animation.webp` from the WebP tools. It converts a GIF to WebP and offers -lossy and -mixed options, where mixed picks lossy or lossless for each frame.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick animation.gif -coalesce animation.webp`. The -coalesce option fully defines the look of each frame of a GIF animation, and your ImageMagick needs WebP support, so check its format list.

### Problems with GIF files

- **The WebP is a single picture**: that is how this page works. Use one of the command-line methods above to try for the motion.
- **The first frame is not what you expected**: this page converts only the first frame, so pick the frame in an editor and save it as its own picture first.
- **Soft edges look jagged**: GIF transparency is on or off, so a soft shadow can't be partly see-through. The WebP can't add that back.
- **Colors look blotchy**: the 256-color palette is the cause. GIMP also limits a GIF export to 256 colors, which alters gradients.
- **Frames overlap or leave trails after an edit**: frame disposal sets how later images cover earlier ones. Pick combine or replace in GIMP to match the animation.
- **An old browser balks at the WebP**: a browser from some years back can show still WebP yet lack animation support. Convert the first frame to PNG or JPG if a viewer will not open it.
- **A comment you wrote in the GIF is gone**: GIMP drops a GIF comment with characters outside seven-bit ASCII, and this page drops metadata altogether.

guide.title: About HEIC files
guide.markdown:
### What is a HEIC file?

A HEIC file is a photo stored in HEIF, the High Efficiency Image File Format, with its pictures compressed by HEVC, the H.265 video codec. HEIF is a container standard from MPEG, ISO/IEC 23008-12, first published in 2017. Apple made it the iPhone's photo format with iOS 11 and macOS High Sierra, and the iPhone 7 and later capture in it. Apple says HEIF compresses photos better than JPEG.

One HEIF file can hold more than one picture. It can carry several images or an image sequence, an alpha channel stored as an extra image, more than 8 bits per color channel, and Exif or XMP metadata.

On an iPhone set to High Efficiency, new photos are HEIC. Copied to a computer over USB, they can arrive as JPEG instead, unless Keep Originals is chosen in the Photos settings. Some Android phones can save HEIF too, from Android 10 on devices that support it.

### Programs that open HEIC files

- **Windows:** Microsoft Photos opens HEIC once both the HEIF Image Extension and the HEVC Video Extensions are installed from the Microsoft Store.
- **Windows and Linux:** GIMP imports HEIC. ImageMagick reads it too, with the libheif delegate.
- **Windows and Mac:** Adobe Photoshop opens HEIC on macOS 10.13 or later, and on Windows once both Microsoft codecs are installed.
- **Mac:** Apple Preview opens HEIF and exports JPEG or PNG, from macOS High Sierra 10.13; Photos, on Mac and mobile, also opens HEIF and exports another format.
- **Web and mobile:** Safari displays HEIC images from version 17.
- **Web:** the signed-in OneDrive website previews uploaded HEIF.
- **Mobile:** on Android, HEIF decoding starts at version 9.

### HEIC and JPG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .heic or .heif, with image/heic and image/heif; .jpg or .jpeg, with image/jpeg.
- **Compression**: HEIC pictures are coded with HEVC (H.265). Baseline JPEG cuts the picture into 8x8 tiles, applies a discrete cosine transform to each tile and Huffman-codes the result.
- **What one file holds**: a HEIF can bundle several images and an alpha channel. A JPG holds one picture.
- **Color depth**: HEIF allows high bit depths; JPEG stores 8 bits per channel. This page decodes to 8-bit pixels.
- **Transparency**: a JPG has no alpha channel at all.
- **Metadata**: a HEIF can carry Exif or XMP. The JPG made here doesn't get the HEIC's Exif data or ICC profile.
- **Quality setting**: the same quality figure gives different output from one tool to the next. This page writes each JPG at 0.85, where 1 is the top of the scale.
- **Where it opens**: JPEG displays in each major browser, and cameras and scanners tend to produce it. HEIC needs the support listed above.

The trade is reach for fidelity. Every major browser displays the JPG, and the page asks for no extension. It is lossy at quality 0.85, and it carries none of the HEIC's Exif tags. A HEIC that holds several images gives only its primary picture.

### Other ways to convert HEIC to JPG

- **Finder (Mac):** Control-click the photo, choose Quick Actions > Convert Image, then choose JPEG and a size.
- **Preview (Mac):** open the photo, choose File > Export, and change Format to JPEG.
- **Photos (Mac):** select the photos, choose File > Export > Export Photos, then set Photo Kind to JPEG.
- **iPhone camera setting:** Settings > Camera > Formats > Most Compatible makes new photos JPEG. Photos you already took stay HEIC.

### Problems with HEIC files

- **Windows says it can't open the file**: add the two Microsoft Store codecs, the HEIF and HEVC extensions, or convert here instead.
- **A website won't accept it**: convert it to JPG here, or use the [HEIC to PNG converter](/heic-to-png/) to get a PNG.
- **The page says "No images in HEIF"**: the file contains nothing to decode. Copy the photo off the phone again and retry.
- **HEIC on one computer, JPG on another**: a USB import from an iPhone can produce JPEG instead. Choose Keep Originals in the Photos settings to get the HEIC files.
- **A whole album to convert**: choose all the photos at once. Each JPG downloads as soon as it's ready.
- **The JPG shows less detail than the HEIC**: both formats are lossy, so a conversion can cost some detail. Convert from the original HEIC, not from a copy that was already converted.
- **A HEIC from an Android phone**: some Android phones save HEIF, and this page converts those files the same way.
