guide.title: About TGA and PNG
guide.markdown:
### What is a TGA file?

Targa, or TGA, is a raster format that Truevision introduced in 1984. Each pixel takes 8 to 32 bits, run-length encoding is optional, and an alpha channel may be included. It has a simple header, and ImageMagick's format list marks it as readable and writable.

Targa survives in game development and in video and 3D rendering, where artists and tools still pass textures and renders around as TGA. ImageMagick groups the ICB, VDA and VST endings with Truevision Targa, so those files are the same family.

### Programs that open TGA files

- **Linux, Mac and Windows:** the Targa plug-in that ships with GIMP loads and exports TGA images.
- **Linux, Mac and Windows:** ImageMagick can read and write Truevision Targa, which covers the TGA, ICB, VDA and VST family.
- **Windows and Mac:** Adobe Photoshop opens Targa images and provides Targa save options.

### TGA and PNG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .tga (also .icb, .vda, .vst) for Targa; .png and image/png for PNG.
- **Compression**: Targa's run-length encoding is optional. PNG always compresses, using DEFLATE (LZ77 plus Huffman coding), and it is lossless.
- **Color depth**: Targa runs from 8 to 32 bits per pixel. PNG supports indexed, grayscale and truecolor images with 1 to 16 bits per sample.
- **Transparency**: both have an alpha channel.
- **Used for**: Targa serves game textures and video and 3D rendering output. PNG is the choice for sharp web graphics, interface art, logos and screenshots, and for pictures that need transparency.
- **Origin**: Targa dates from 1984, and PNG from the mid-1990s, when it was devised as a patent-free successor to GIF. October 1996 saw it become the W3C's first published Recommendation for an image format. Its standards-body editions are RFC 2083 and ISO/IEC 15948:2004.
- **Reach**: browsers of every major kind show PNG, and no known patent on it demands royalties. GIMP, Windows Photos and Preview on macOS open it too, and macOS saves screenshots in PNG by default.
- **Media types**: image/png is registered for PNG, and image/apng for animated files.
- **Structure**: inside a PNG you find a fixed signature and then a run of chunks; the header lives in IHDR, image data sits in IDAT and IEND ends the file.
- **Newer features**: software without animation support shows PNG's default still image, though the specification itself now covers animated PNG. The third edition adds HDR support via a cICP chunk and Exif metadata in an eXIf chunk.

Mostly the wrapper changes here. ImageMagick compiled to WebAssembly reads the TGA and writes a PNG, and the page passes no quality setting. The file is read as a single image, and nothing is uploaded. A picture over about 537 megapixels is turned away. Your original TGA is not changed, since you download a new copy. When you pick several files, they are handled one at a time and no ZIP is made.

### Other ways to convert TGA to PNG

- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick texture.tga texture.png`. ImageMagick's format list shows TGA and PNG as both readable and writable, and its quickstart shows the same pattern: `magick rose.jpg rose.png`.
- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux):** open the TGA with File > Open, then pick File > Export As and give it the name texture.png. The PNG dialog that follows lists pixel format and metadata options. The compression level only trades speed for size, since PNG compression is not lossy.
- **IrfanView:** choose File > Open for the Targa, then File > Save as and select PNG. IrfanView's format list marks TGA and PNG as readable and savable, and its FAQ says to set the new file name or folder and save.

### Problems with TGA files

- **An indexed TGA with transparency looks wrong in one program**: programs differ here. GIMP 2.10.32 improved its support for indexed Targa images with an alpha channel, on both import and export.
- **A tool rejects the file by its ending**: the ICB, VDA and VST endings name Truevision Targa too, but this page's file picker lists .tga files.
- **The page calls the picture too large**: reduce the render's pixel count in an editor, then convert again.
- **The PNG has a different file size**: Targa's run-length encoding is optional and PNG always compresses. PNG compression is lossless, so a different size is not a quality loss.
- **A file with several images gives one picture**: only a single image is taken from the file.

faqs.question: How do I change a TIF to a JPG?
faqs.answer: Drop your TIF on the converter above. ImageMagick opens it inside your browser, and a JPG copy downloads when it is done. The original TIF is left as it was.

faqs.question: Can I turn a stack of TIF scans into JPGs?
faqs.answer: Select several TIFs in the picker and they convert in sequence. Every JPG is saved on its own under the TIF's name and no archive is made, so a big batch means many downloads.

faqs.question: What happens to a TIF with several pages?
faqs.answer: Only one image is read from the file, so the result is a single JPG and not one per page. A TIFF can hold several images, which is why it suits scanned document sequences.

faqs.question: Are .tif and .tiff the same?
faqs.answer: Yes. Both spellings name TIFF, short for Tagged Image File Format, whose media type is image/tiff. The file picker on this page lists .tif files.

faqs.question: Can I convert TIF to JPG without losing quality?
faqs.answer: No. JPEG discards detail, and there is no quality setting here to turn up. Store the TIF as the master and send out the JPG.

faqs.question: Why did my TIF fail to convert?
faqs.answer: A damaged file, or a TIFF variant that ImageMagick cannot read, ends with a message that the picture couldn't be read.

faqs.question: Is my TIF uploaded to a server?
faqs.answer: No. The conversion runs inside your browser tab, so the scan never leaves your device. Only the finished JPG is saved.

faqs.question: Should I pick PNG instead of JPG for a TIF?
faqs.answer: Pick PNG through the [TIF to PNG converter](/tif-to-png/) when every pixel must survive, since PNG is lossless. Choose JPG when a small file that opens anywhere matters more.

faqs.question: Will a very large TIF stop the conversion?
faqs.answer: File size is not capped. Only a picture with an extreme pixel count is refused, with a message that it is too big for this page.

faqs.question: Does the JPG keep my TIF's file name?
faqs.answer: Yes, apart from the ending. scan.tif downloads as scan.jpg.

guide.title: About TIF files
guide.markdown:
### What is a TIF file?

TIF is the short spelling of TIFF, the Tagged Image File Format. It is a raster format first published by Aldus in 1986 and developed with Microsoft, and Adobe now holds its specification. Revision 6.0 came out in 1992. A TIFF is built from tags that say how the pixel data is stored, so two files with the same ending can differ a lot inside.

That flexibility is why scanners, print shops and document-imaging systems use it. A TIFF can use different compression methods and color representations, reach high bit depths, and hold several images in one file, which suits a scanned stack of pages. It is not always lossless, though. The compression is chosen when the file is written.

Photographers and archivists keep TIFFs as preservation masters because high bit depth and lossless storage are established uses of the format. The ending tells you the container, not what is in it: one page or fifty, 8 bits or 16, lossless or not.

### Programs that open TIF files

- **Linux, Mac and Windows:** TIFF opens in GIMP for editing. ImageMagick reads and writes TIFF from the command line, with controls for compression, strips, tiles and byte order.
- **Windows:** Windows Photos opens TIFF.
- **Mac:** Preview lists TIFF among the formats in File > Export, and Adobe Photoshop opens TIFF too.

### TIF and JPG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .tif and .tiff with image/tiff; .jpg and .jpeg with image/jpeg.
- **Compression**: a TIFF can be lossless or lossy, depending on the method used. JPG is always lossy, so detail is traded for a smaller file.
- **Pages**: a TIFF can hold several images. A JPG is one picture, and this page writes one JPG for each file.
- **Bit depth and color**: TIFF can carry high bit depths and CMYK. The converter works at 8 bits for the JPG.
- **Specification**: Adobe controls the TIFF specification, while JPEG is defined by the ISO/IEC 10918-1 standard.
- **Support**: JPG is supported almost everywhere, and every major browser displays it.

ISO/IEC 10918-1, published in 1994, is the core JPEG standard, written by the Joint Photographic Experts Group. Digital cameras and scanners generally produce it natively. A 0 to 100 range is typical, but identical figures can look different between programs. Progressive JPEGs paint a blurry preview first and sharpen it as the remaining data arrives.

The conversion sets no quality, so there is nothing to tune here. For a scan of fine print or line art, look at the JPG at full size before you throw anything away. The TIF on your disk stays as it was; what you download is a fresh JPG that carries its name. Picking several TIFs together runs them one after another with no ZIP. A lossless copy is also possible, because the site has a PNG option for TIF files.

### Other ways to convert TIF to JPG

- **GIMP:** open the TIFF and choose File > Export As. The Quality field in GIMP's JPEG export dialog accepts 0 to 100. GIMP's manual says every format other than XCF loses some image properties, such as layers and transparency, and that exporting does not change the open image.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick scan.tif scan-copy.jpg`. ImageMagick's format list marks TIFF as readable and writable. In a test with a small TIF this wrote a JPG.

### Problems with TIF files

- **A website or form rejects the TIF**: convert the file. Renaming it to .jpg does not change what is inside.
- **Only one picture came out**: a TIFF can hold several images, and this page gives one JPG per file. Use software that exposes the full image sequence if you need every page.
- **A reader does not understand the file**: private tags vary, and a program may not recognize all of them, color-profile extensions included.
- **The page says the picture couldn't be read**: either the file is damaged or it uses a TIFF variant that ImageMagick cannot decode. Try the scanning software that made it.

guide.title: About TIF files
guide.markdown:
### What is a TIF file?

A .tif file holds a TIFF, short for Tagged Image File Format. Aldus and Microsoft created it, and the specification now belongs to Adobe, which acquired Aldus's PageMaker program. Aldus first published TIFF in 1986. At that point it handled only bilevel images, and grayscale and color came later as scanners and storage improved. Revision 6.0 arrived in 1992, and files that follow earlier versions remain valid TIFF 6.0 files.

You meet a .tif when you scan a document, when a photographer or print shop sends a print master, or when a library or archive hands over a preservation copy. Among the Library of Congress's preferred formats for photographs and other graphic images is TIFF, which it uses as a master format in many digitization workflows. Subtypes such as TIFF/EP, GeoTIFF and Adobe DNG build on it. The long .tiff ending names the identical format, and image/tiff is the media type for both.

### Programs that open TIF files

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- GIMP: opens a scan for editing, and each export format keeps its own subset of the project's properties.

**Mac**

- Preview: has TIFF in its File > Export menu among the formats it can write.

### TIF and PNG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .tif or .tiff with image/tiff, and .png with image/png.
- **Compression**: a TIFF may be stored uncompressed or with LZW, Group 4 or JPEG, whereas PNG never loses data.
- **Images per file**: one TIF can contain many pictures, which suits a stack of scanned pages. This page reads only a single picture from the file.
- **Color**: color handling is defined by a tag. Plain 8-bit grayscale and 24-bit RGB dominate, yet some workflows go past 8 bits per channel. An embedded ICC profile is possible in a TIF, though not every reader recognizes it, so the format suits high-bit-depth imaging and preservation masters. PNG offers 8-bit and 16-bit channels plus alpha transparency.
- **Age**: TIFF dates from 1986 and grew up with scanning and print. PNG was designed in the mid-1990s to replace GIF without its patent problems, and it is now both a W3C Recommendation and ISO/IEC 15948.
- **Reach**: every browser draws a PNG, while a TIF needs a program that understands it.

On this page ImageMagick runs as WebAssembly inside your browser, so your scan is never sent to a server. It decodes one picture from the TIF and writes it as a PNG, without resizing it or setting a quality value. Only the first file waits for the converter to load. A multi-page TIF gives a single PNG rather than one per page. When you need every page, keep the TIF as your master and treat the PNG as a viewing copy.

### Other ways to convert TIF to PNG

- **Preview (Mac):** open the TIF, choose File > Export, set the Format menu to PNG and press Save. That menu offers PNG next to HEIC, JPEG, JPEG-2000, OpenEXR, PDF and TIFF. For many files, open them in one Preview window, select them in the sidebar and export.
- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux):** open the scan, choose File > Export As, type .png after the name in the Name field, then press Export.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick 'scan.tif[0]' scan.png`. The number in brackets selects one image from a multi-image file, counting from zero, so `[1]` is the second. Keep the quotes, since Linux shells treat brackets specially.

### Problems with TIF files

- **A program shows just one image of a multi-page scan**: a TIFF may hold several images, and only software that exposes the whole sequence shows them all. Open the file in such a program, or choose a page with ImageMagick as above.
- **The conversion stops with a size error**: anything over about 537 megapixels is turned back, and you can shrink the scan's resolution in an editor first. Classic TIFF itself tops out near 4 GB because of its 32-bit offsets, and BigTIFF uses 64-bit offsets to lift that.
- **Colors or tags look wrong elsewhere**: some private tags, including certain color-profile extensions, are unknown to other readers. Export from the program that made the TIF.
- **A renamed file still fails**: switching .tif to .png leaves TIFF data inside, so make a real conversion.

guide.title: About TIFF and JPG files
guide.markdown:
### What is a TIFF file?

Short for Tagged Image File Format, TIFF is a tag-based raster wrapper created by Aldus and Microsoft. The first release dates from 1986 and revision 6.0 from 1992; Adobe now controls the specification. TIFF permits several compression methods and several color representations. Files end in .tif or .tiff, and the media type is image/tiff.

Multiple images per file make TIFF useful for scanned document sequences, and high bit depth imaging and preservation masters are established uses. You meet TIFF from scanners, in print and professional photography workflows, and as the master copy a photographer keeps beside a smaller JPG. The format reference also lists fax and document imaging among its uses. GIMP supports high-precision TIFF import and export. Because a TIFF may hold several images, a converter that reads one has to take a single image from the file.

### Programs that open TIFF files

**Mac**

- Preview: the format list under File > Export offers TIFF.

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- GIMP: imports TIFF for editing, and what an export keeps depends on the format.
- ImageMagick: reads and writes TIFF; compression, strips, tiles and byte order are all adjustable.

**Windows**

- Windows Photos: the format reference lists it.

### TIFF and JPG compared

- **Extensions**: .tif or .tiff is image/tiff, while .jpg or .jpeg is image/jpeg.
- **Compression**: TIFF can be lossless or lossy. JPEG is lossy: the picture is divided into 8x8 blocks that go through a discrete cosine transform before Huffman coding.
- **Pages**: a TIFF may contain several images, whereas a JPG is a single picture.
- **Color depth**: TIFF supports high bit depth and CMYK. JPEG stores 8 bits per color channel.
- **Transparency**: JPEG has no alpha channel. Layers do not survive either.
- **Size limit**: classic TIFF is capped near 4 GB.
- **Support**: JPG opens in every browser and phone. TIFF needs a viewer that understands its tags.
- **Typical use**: TIFF for scanning, archiving and print. JPG for web photos, camera output and email attachments.
- **Quality setting**: TIFF has none for lossless compression. JPEG quality runs from 0 to 100, but programs scale it differently, so equal numbers do not give equal results.

ImageMagick takes one image from the TIFF and saves a JPG. A multi-page TIFF gives one picture, not one per page. Keep the TIFF: a JPG cannot be turned back into it, and saving the JPG again later costs more detail.

The download takes the TIFF's name with .jpg in place of .tif or .tiff, and each TIFF in a batch is converted and saved on its own.

### Other ways to convert TIFF to JPG

- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux):** load the TIFF, go to File > Export As, pick the JPEG entry in the file types and hit Export. The JPEG settings dialog appears next, where the default quality is 85.
- **Preview (Mac):** open the TIFF, go to File > Export, choose JPEG as the Format and save.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick 'input.tiff[0]' output.jpg`. The [0] picks the first image in the file, and the quotes keep the brackets away from the shell.

On a desktop you can set the JPEG quality and see the settings before saving, which this page does not offer.

### Problems with TIFF files

- **It will not open**: viewers can stumble on private tags, some color-profile extensions included. Re-save it from GIMP or a similar editor.
- **Only one page converted**: the TIFF holds several images and this page reads one. Use software that exposes the whole image sequence.
- **Over 4 GB**: classic TIFF uses 32-bit offsets and stops at about 4 GB, and BigTIFF extends those fields.
- **The picture is too large**: pictures over roughly 537 megapixels are refused.
- **A "couldn't be read" message**: the page could not read the picture, which may be damaged or incomplete; save a new TIFF from GIMP or Preview and convert that.
- **Transparent areas change**: a JPG cannot keep transparency. Convert to PNG if you need it.
- **A scanned page looks soft**: JPEG is lossy and works in 8x8 blocks, so thin lines and small text can blur. Keep the TIFF as the master.
- **The colors look off**: a JPG holds 8 bits per channel, so a high bit depth TIFF is reduced. Check the result against the original.

Both .tif and .tiff are used for it, and its media type is image/tiff.

Deep bit depths and preservation masters are also long-standing uses. You mostly meet it from scanners, fax and document imaging software, and in professional photography and print. A PDF is a common next step when a scan has to be sent or filed. It turns the image into a document page that PDF readers handle.

- **Extensions**: .tif and .tiff are image/tiff, .pdf is application/pdf.
- **Pages**: one TIFF file may contain several images, while a PDF holds fixed pages; this page writes a single page.
- **Compression**: TIFF can be lossless or lossy, and offers many methods. This page embeds the picture in the PDF losslessly.
- **Content**: a TIFF holds raster pixels alone. A PDF can combine text, vector graphics and images, though the PDF written here carries a single picture.
- **Color depth**: TIFF can use high bit depth and CMYK. PDF images can use lossless Flate compression or JPEG.
- **Size limit**: classic TIFF uses 32-bit offsets, which keeps it to about 4 GB. BigTIFF extends those fields.

### What is a TIFF file?

TIFF is short for Tagged Image File Format, a design whose point is its tags. A file opens with a header, followed by one or more directories of tags, each directory with its own bitmap data; a directory and its bitmap form a subfile. That structure is how a TIFF holds a run of scanned pages. The tags define color, bit depth and compression, and Adobe keeps a registry of extensions. Some private tags, including color-profile extensions, mean nothing to certain readers.

Two endings, .tiff and .tif, point to this one format, which is registered as image/tiff. The Library of Congress describes the format as fully documented and free of external dependencies, and it is on the preferred list for photographs and other graphic images. TIFF/IT, TIFF/EP and GeoTIFF are subtypes that extend it, and camera Exif metadata shows up in TIFF/EP files. Aldus and Microsoft created TIFF; today Adobe controls the specification, having acquired Aldus's PageMaker program. It began in 1986 as a bilevel format. Version 6.0 was published in 1992, and TIFF 5.0 is still used for many uncompressed images.

### Programs that open TIFF files

**Windows, Linux and Mac**

- ImageMagick: handles TIFF in both directions, with settings for strips, tiles, byte order and compression.

**Mac**

- Preview: TIFF is among the file types offered under File > Export.

### TIFF and PNG compared

- **Names and types**: .tiff or .tif carry image/tiff; .png carries image/png.
- **Compression**: a TIFF can be stored raw, or use LZW, Group 4 (a CCITT scheme for black-and-white images) or JPEG. The LZW patent expired in 2003 in the U.S. and in 2004 in Europe and Japan. PNG compression is lossless.
- **Pages**: a TIFF can hold several images, handy for scanned sequences, but this page reads one picture from the file.
- **Color**: the Photometric Interpretation tag picks the color space. 8-bit grayscale and 24-bit RGB are widespread, though a few TIFF workflows exceed 8 bits per channel. PNG provides 8-bit and 16-bit channels.
- **Transparency**: only PNG offers an alpha channel here.
- **Size ceiling**: classic TIFF uses 32-bit offsets and stops near 4 GB, while BigTIFF uses 64-bit offsets.
- **Background**: TIFF is the older format, built around scanners and print. PNG followed in the mid-1990s as a GIF replacement without patent worries, and it became ISO/IEC 15948 and a W3C Recommendation.

The page decodes one picture with ImageMagick, running as WebAssembly inside your browser, and writes it as a PNG. It does not resize the picture or set a quality value, and the TIFF itself is never altered. If your TIFF is a multi-page scan or a print master, treat the PNG as a copy to share rather than a replacement.

### Other ways to convert TIFF to PNG

- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick 'master.tiff[0]' copy.png`. Put a different frame number in the brackets, counting from zero, to reach a later page. The quotes matter because Linux shells interpret brackets.
- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux):** open the TIFF, pick File > Export As, make the Name field end in .png and click Export.
- **Preview (Mac):** open the TIFF, pick File > Export, select PNG in the Format menu, then press Save. A batch works if you open the files in one Preview window and select them in the sidebar.

### Problems with TIFF files

- **Only the first page came out**: a TIFF can hold many images but this page reads only one. Use ImageMagick with a page number as shown, or software that exposes the whole sequence.
- **The picture is rejected as too large**: beyond about 537 megapixels the page refuses it. Lower the scan's resolution in an editor and retry.
- **A program reads it wrongly**: readers differ over private tags. Open the file in the software that created it and export a standard copy.
- **The file is near 4 GB**: classic TIFF can't grow past that because of its 32-bit offsets, which is what BigTIFF was made to fix.
- **The color profile is missing**: ICC profiles live in an extension tag that not every reader recognizes, so check the result in a second viewer before deleting the original.
- **A renamed file still fails**: changing .tiff to .png leaves TIFF data inside, so run an actual conversion.

faqs.question: How do I convert TS to MP4?
faqs.answer: Pick your .ts file on this page. FFmpeg re-encodes the stream into an MP4 inside your browser, and you save the result. The recording stays on your device.

faqs.question: How do I convert .ts to MP4 on my computer?
faqs.answer: Rewrap it with FFmpeg's stream copy, `-c copy`, with no re-encoding, or open the file in HandBrake or VLC and choose MP4. This page does the re-encode in the browser instead.

faqs.question: Is converting TS to MP4 lossless?
faqs.answer: On this page, no. The video is encoded again with x264 at CRF 32 and the audio as AAC at 96 kbps. The FFmpeg copy method on your computer doesn't re-encode, so it keeps the streams as they are when MP4 can hold them.

faqs.question: Will my 4K recording stay 4K?
faqs.answer: No. The picture is kept within 1920 px on the longer side and 30 fps. Dimensions are forced to even values, so a picture with an odd height comes out one pixel shorter.

faqs.question: Why does the MP4 start playing before it finishes loading?
faqs.answer: The page adds `+faststart`, which puts the index at the start of the file. Browsers can then begin playback early.

faqs.question: Which video and audio streams does the MP4 get?
faqs.answer: FFmpeg's defaults choose them, because the page maps no streams. The command has no `-map_metadata` option, so the input's global tags, such as the title, go into an output that has fields for them.

faqs.question: Why is the converted video softer than the broadcast?
faqs.answer: The encode is tuned for speed and size: ultrafast preset, CRF 32. That trades detail for a smaller file and a quicker run. Interlaced pictures also get a deinterlace filter.

faqs.question: Can I convert more than one TS recording?
faqs.answer: Yes, select them together. Each recording is processed in turn and saved as a separate MP4; they are not joined.

faqs.question: Does it work for a very long recording?
faqs.answer: Neither size nor running time is capped. A long recording keeps your device busy longer, and FFmpeg's single thread in the browser adds to the wait.

faqs.question: Why does the TS file not play in my browser?
faqs.answer: A transport stream is a system format for broadcast, and browsers play MP4 instead. Converting gives you the file they know.

guide.title: About TS files
guide.markdown:
### What is a TS file?

TS identifies an MPEG-2 transport stream, one of the system formats specified by ISO/IEC 13818-1. A transport stream doesn't define a picture codec. It multiplexes separately coded video and sound, and one stream can carry several programs with independent clocks. Its syntax uses timestamps to coordinate presentation and decoder buffering. Broadcast distribution and transmissions vulnerable to errors are important uses of TS. Besides television, TS is used for HLS segments in streaming and for footage from Blu-ray discs and camcorders, and its fixed 188-byte packets help streams survive transmission errors.

The usual extension is .ts and the registered media type is video/mp2t. You tend to meet it as a recording from a TV tuner, a stream or a capture, where the file is long and not tidy.

MP4 is the MPEG-4 Part 14 format, ISO/IEC 14496-14, first published in 2003. Typically it holds H.264 video and AAC audio, and all major browsers play it. That is the reason for the conversion: MP4 opens in places a .ts file doesn't. Because TS is a wrapper rather than a codec, the video inside may already be H.264. Even so, this page encodes it again, so the result is a new file with its own quality settings, not a copy of the original streams.

### Programs that open TS files

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- FFmpeg: reads transport streams.
- VLC media player: its input list includes TS.

**Mobile**

- Android: the VLC app lists TS among its inputs, and decoding depends on the stream's media.

### TS and MP4 compared

- **What it is**: TS is a system format for multiplexed streams and broadcast. MP4 is a file container built on the ISO Base Media File Format.
- **Codecs**: neither fixes the codec. An MP4 often has H.264 and AAC, and may use AV1, VP9, MP3 or Opus instead.
- **Programs**: one TS can carry several programs. An MP4 normally holds one movie.
- **Playback**: browsers play MP4; a .ts file needs a player that understands transport streams.
- **Timing**: a TS leans on timestamps for presentation and decoder buffering, which suits a broadcast that may lose packets. An MP4 is built for files you store and play back.
- **Extensions and types**: .ts and video/mp2t; .mp4 or .m4v and video/mp4.

This page encodes new video. In your browser, FFmpeg uses `libx264` (preset ultrafast, CRF 32, tune zerolatency) for video and AAC at 96 kbps for audio, adds `+faststart` so the MP4 can start before it has fully loaded, and applies a deinterlace filter (`yadif`). The longer side stays at or under 1920 px and the frame rate at or under 30 fps. Sides round down to even numbers, which costs an odd dimension one pixel. No `-map` is passed, so FFmpeg's defaults pick the streams.

### Other ways to convert TS to MP4

- **FFmpeg, copy:** run `ffmpeg -i input.ts -c copy output.mp4`. It doesn't re-encode, so the streams stay as they are, but MP4 must be able to hold them.
- **HandBrake:** choose Open Source, pick a preset, set the file name in Save As and the folder in To, then press Start. HandBrake's container page says it may switch an MP4 to the .m4v ending when AC3 pass-through, SRT subtitles or chapter markers are on, and a preference turns that off.
- **VLC:** under Media > Convert/Save, add the recording, select the Video - H.264 + MP3 (MP4) profile, name a destination and start. The profile's name says MP3 sound.

### Problems with TS files

- **It won't play in a browser**: browsers read MP4 rather than TS, so this is expected and not a fault in the file.
- **The codec isn't supported**: recognizing the TS wrapper doesn't settle which codec decodes its audio or video.
- **Glitches or jumps in the picture**: a TS is built to survive transmission errors, but lost packets can still leave flaws. The MP4 follows the stream as written, so it shows the same flaws. Try another copy of the recording.
- **The MP4 is smaller than the TS**: the picture is capped in size and frame rate, and CRF 32 compresses hard.
- **Fine detail looks worse**: the video is encoded again. Convert from the original TS each time.
- **A long recording is slow**: the conversion is single-threaded in your browser, so a longer file means a longer wait.

faqs.question: How can I turn a TXT file into a PDF?
faqs.answer: Pick the TXT file, and the PDF is built in your browser, then downloads with the same name and a .pdf ending. The text is set on A4 pages, so there are no settings to change.

faqs.question: What font and page size does the PDF use?
faqs.answer: A4 portrait with 3/4 inch margins. A file of plain Windows-1252 text gets Courier, and any other file gets DejaVu Sans.

faqs.question: Will my columns and spacing line up?
faqs.answer: In Courier they do, because every character has the same width. Leading spaces and blank lines are kept. In DejaVu Sans each letter has its own width, so spaced-out columns drift, though indentation still lines up.

faqs.question: What happens to lines that are longer than the page?
faqs.answer: They wrap, first between words and, for a word too long for a line, inside the word. The continuation lines are indented as far as the line itself, up to 40 columns.

faqs.question: Can I choose where pages break?
faqs.answer: Put a form feed character where you want a new page and the PDF starts a new page there, as a printer would. Files paginated that way, such as old RFCs and reports, keep their pages.

faqs.question: Why is my Chinese, Japanese or emoji text refused?
faqs.answer: The font has no glyphs for those characters, so the page names the characters it can't set instead of printing blanks. The [TXT to PNG converter](/txt-to-png/) draws them, though it makes a picture rather than a PDF.

faqs.question: Why do accents or non-English letters look wrong?
faqs.answer: The page reads UTF-8 or UTF-16 by the byte order mark, then tries UTF-8, then Windows-1252. A file saved in another legacy encoding, such as Shift_JIS or KOI8-R, is read as Windows-1252 and set that way.

faqs.question: Is there a size limit?
faqs.answer: Yes: a file over 20 MB is refused before it is read, and so is one that would run past 2,000 pages. 2,000 full pages hold about 10 million characters.

faqs.question: Can I add page numbers or a header?
faqs.answer: No. The page adds nothing but your text. For headers, footers or numbering, use a word processor and export a PDF from there.

faqs.question: Does the PDF have selectable text?
faqs.answer: Yes. The text is set as real text in the PDF, so you can search it and copy from it. The PDF is titled with the file's name.

guide.title: About TXT and PDF files
guide.markdown:
### What is a TXT file?

A TXT file is plain text: characters and line endings, with no fonts, styles, tables or pictures. Its media type is text/plain, and a charset parameter says how the bytes stand for characters. Plain text carries no commands for typography and sets no page layout, which is why any editor on any system can open it and why the files stay small.

You find .txt files as notes, logs, readme files, exported data and the text of old documents. Because there is no layout, there is no page size either. That is the gap a PDF fills: it turns the same lines into fixed pages that print and look the same on every device.

Line endings differ by system, so a TXT may end its lines with CR LF, CR or LF. This page treats all three as a line break, along with NEL and the Unicode line and paragraph separators. It reads the encoding from a byte order mark when there is one: UTF-8 or UTF-16. Without one it tries UTF-8 and then Windows-1252.

### Programs that open TXT files

**Windows**

- Notepad: the format reference's first choice for plain text.

**Mac**

- TextEdit: handles plain text documents, including opening, editing and saving them.

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- Visual Studio Code: opens and edits text files in its editor.
- Vim: a text editor that runs on all three.

### TXT and PDF compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .txt with text/plain, against .pdf with application/pdf.
- **Layout**: a TXT has none. A PDF is a set of fixed pages that look the same everywhere.
- **Fonts**: a TXT uses whatever font the viewer picks. A PDF embeds its fonts to keep its look.
- **Content**: a TXT holds text only. Beyond text, a PDF can carry vector graphics and images, along with links, bookmarks and forms.
- **Standards**: ISO adopted PDF 1.7 as ISO 32000-1 in 2008; PDF 2.0 followed as ISO 32000-2 in 2017.

This page sets your text on A4 portrait pages with 3/4 inch margins, in Courier at 10 pt with 12 pt between lines. That gives 61 lines to a page, each up to 81 characters, about what an 80-column printout holds. Nothing else is added.

Tabs stop at every fourth column, control characters and terminal escape sequences are dropped, and a line whose first letter is Hebrew or Arabic is set against the right margin, as an editor shows it. All-Windows-1252 text gets Courier; any other text gets DejaVu Sans, which has a wider range of letters but gives each its own width.

The PDF text is real text, not a picture of it, so a PDF reader can search and copy it.

### Other ways to convert TXT to PDF

- **TextEdit (Mac):** open the TXT, then choose File > Export as PDF. TextEdit lays the page out with its own settings, not a fixed grid of lines.
- **Adobe Acrobat:** use File > Create > PDF from File, change the file-type filter in the Open dialog so TXT files show, pick the file, press Open and save the result. The layout follows Acrobat's settings.

Use a word processor route when you want your own fonts, headers or page numbers.

### Problems with TXT files

- **Accents or symbols turn into odd characters**: the file was saved in a different encoding from the one it is read in. Re-save it as UTF-8.
- **A line is cut off in the PDF**: it is not cut. Lines longer than 81 characters wrap onto the next line, indented to match.
- **Text in Chinese, Japanese, Korean or emoji is refused**: the PDF font lacks those glyphs. Use TXT to PNG, which draws them.
- **The file is rejected as empty**: a file with only whitespace and control characters has nothing to set.
- **Tabs look narrow**: tabs stop every fourth column in the PDF, so a file written for eight-column tabs will look tighter than in your editor.
- **Columns drift**: the file has characters beyond Windows-1252, so the whole text was set in DejaVu Sans, where spaces do not line up columns. Remove those characters to get Courier.
- **A report keeps its page breaks only sometimes**: a form feed ends a page that has a line on it, but does nothing on a page with none.

guide.title: About video to GIF
guide.markdown:
### What is an MP4 file?

The MPEG-4 Part 14 specification, ISO/IEC 14496-14, defines MP4 and dates from 2003. A typical MP4 holds H.264 video and AAC audio, yet containers of this kind take AV1, VP9, MP3 and Opus too. The ISO Base Media File Format underlies MP4, and QuickTime is where that format came from. An MP4 consists of nested boxes, which QuickTime calls atoms.

Video uses the endings .mp4 or .m4v, while MPEG-4 files with audio alone often end in .m4a. The registered media types are video/mp4 and audio/mp4, and every major browser plays MP4. It turns up in online video, recordings from phones and cameras, and shared clips. Its properties include subtitles and chapters, and the usual video codecs are H.264, H.265 and AV1.

### Programs that open MP4 files

**Mobile, Windows, Mac and Linux**

- VLC: plays MP4, MOV and 3GP among its input formats. On phones there are VLC for Android and VLC for iOS, and the container's contents decide what they can decode.

**Linux, Mac and Windows**

- mpv: plays on the desktop and lets you select among its audio and subtitle streams.
- ffplay: the FFmpeg project's own player, which comes with FFmpeg itself, alongside the ffmpeg tool.

**Windows and Mac**

- Adobe Premiere: imports the container if a suitable decoder is installed.

**Windows**

- Windows Media Player: opens MP4 files.

**Mac**

- QuickTime Player: can play MP4 files.

**Web**

- Firefox and Chrome: play supported MP4 directly. The codec inside still matters.

### MP4 and GIF compared

- **Origin**: CompuServe introduced GIF in 1987. GIF89a, from July 1990, introduced extensions covering transparency, timing between frames, comments and application data.
- **Color**: palettes in a GIF image are capped at 256 colors. Transparency designates a single palette entry as fully clear, and nothing is partly transparent.
- **Compression**: GIF uses lossless LZW coding for its images. Unisys started charging for LZW licenses in 1994. In the US the patent ran out in 2003; the European and Japanese ones followed in 2004.
- **Animation**: many images can be stored in one GIF, each with its own delay set in hundredths of a second.
- **Sound**: an MP4 can carry audio. The GIF made here holds pictures only.
- **Uses**: short looping animations, simple graphics, icons, reaction images and stickers suit GIF.
- **Editors**: GIMP can save a multi-layer image as an animated GIF that loops forever, cutting the colors to 256 at most.
- **Support**: All major browsers display GIF; the media type is image/gif.

Process here: on your device, FFmpeg scans the clip once to build a palette and then writes the GIF with it in a second pass. It keeps 15 frames a second and limits the longer side to 480 px, rounding both sides down to an even number. A smaller video is not scaled up. The command also deinterlaces frames marked as interlaced, and sets the GIF to loop forever. FFmpeg runs as WebAssembly in a worker in your browser, so nothing is uploaded. The page has no size or time limit of its own, and a long file simply takes as long as your device needs.

### Other ways to convert MP4 to GIF

- **Microsoft Clipchamp (Windows, web):** put the video in a project, click Export at the top right and pick GIF. Clipchamp offers the GIF export only for videos up to 15 seconds long and accepts MP4 among its containers.
- **FFmpeg (any platform):** the command `ffmpeg -i input.mp4 output.gif` writes a GIF. FFmpeg's GIF muxer loops forever by default, and a frame delay cannot be shorter than one hundredth of a second. This plain command skips the palette step this page uses.

### Problems with MP4 files

- **A player can't show the video**: opening MP4 files doesn't guarantee that a player can decode what is inside.
- **The GIF is too heavy to post**: shorten the clip before converting. Every second adds 15 images, so the file grows with its length.
- **The GIF looks grainy**: each GIF image is limited to 256 colors, which can alter smooth gradients.
- **Your file isn't an MP4**: the file picker takes .mp4 only, so a clip in another container needs its own converter.
- **Your video is another type**: try [MOV to GIF](/mov-to-gif/), or the WebM, AVI and MKV pages.

faqs.question: Why won't my VOB play on its own?

faqs.question: Is there a size limit for VOB files?
faqs.answer: This page has no size cap and no time cap. A large VOB takes longer on a slower computer.

guide.title: Understanding VOB for MP4 output
guide.markdown:
### What is a VOB file?

VOB stands for DVD Video Object. DVD producers store the video, sound, subtitles and menu content of a disc in VOB streams, and the data is closely related to MPEG-2 program-stream material. A VOB can carry several audio and subtitle streams, and it may be encrypted with CSS.

A DVD backup commonly puts the VOB files inside a folder named VIDEO_TS, next to IFO and BUP files that DVD authoring also needs. You meet VOB files on DVD-Video discs and when you rip a disc to files. A single VOB holds up to 1 GB, so a movie longer than that is spread over several, and a disc can hold several titles.

Because a VOB is MPEG-2 material built for a disc, it is awkward outside a player that understands DVDs. Converting the VOBs you want to keep to MP4 gives you ordinary video files that play on nearly every device.

### Programs that open VOB files

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- VLC reads DVD Video media and MPEG program streams.
- HandBrake: opens VOB files and whole VIDEO_TS disc folders, as long as the source is unprotected. Its Title control picks which clip of a multi-clip source, such as a DVD, to use, and it does not defeat copy protection of any kind.

**Windows**

- MPC-HC opens VOB files.
- Windows Media Player opens a VOB when the right codecs are installed.

### VOB and MP4 compared

- **Extensions**: a VOB ends in .vob and sits in a VIDEO_TS folder. An MP4 ends in .mp4 and follows ISO/IEC 14496-14.
- **Format family**: a VOB is built on the MPEG-2 program stream, which FFmpeg's format list names as MPEG-PS, also known as VOB.
- **Streams**: a VOB can hold multiple audio and subtitle streams, and the MP4 container is built for several codecs plus subtitles and chapters.
- **Structure**: a VOB belongs to a set. The IFO and BUP files beside it support DVD authoring. An MP4 is one self-contained file.
- **Subtitles**: DVD subtitle streams can contain bitmap images rather than searchable text.
- **Support**: nearly every device and web browser accepts an MP4, whereas a VOB needs a DVD-aware or MPEG-capable player.
- **Quality**: the MP4 is built from the decoded VOB, so the picture goes through lossy compression a second time.

The VOB is decoded and re-encoded here, with H.264 for the picture and 96 kbps AAC for the sound, and the encoder favors speed over fine detail. Frames flagged as interlaced are deinterlaced, so motion does not comb. A frame up to 1920 px on the longer side keeps its size, apart from rounding each side down to an even number, and a larger frame is scaled down. Video above 30 fps has frames dropped. Several VOBs chosen together are converted one after another, each into its own MP4 named after its VOB. The VOB you choose is left untouched.

### Other ways to convert VOB to MP4

- **FFmpeg (Windows, Mac, Linux):** use `ffmpeg -i clip.vob -c:v libx264 -c:a aac dvd-viewing.mp4`. FFmpeg's format list calls the MPEG program stream the format also known as VOB. The -i flag is the source file, and -c:v and -c:a pick the video and audio encoders, libx264 and aac. If you add nothing else, FFmpeg picks the streams on its own, so the output is not what this page makes.

### Problems with VOB files

- **Only part of the movie plays**: a VOB tops out at 1 GB, so a longer movie runs across several. Convert each one you want and play the MP4s in order.
- **Wrong clip**: a disc source may contain several titles, and choosing the wrong one produces the wrong clip. Check which VOBs belong to the title you want.
- **Copy-protected disc**: HandBrake does not process copy-protected DVD sources, and the format reference notes a VOB may be encrypted with CSS.
- **Menus do not play**: a loose VOB does not replace the full DVD structure, and an MP4 has no disc menus at all.
- **Subtitles missing in a player**: DVD subtitles can be bitmap images, and a player that handles MPEG-2 video may still ignore them.
- **Combing on moving edges**: DVD video is commonly interlaced. Converting here deinterlaces frames flagged that way.

faqs.question: How do I convert WAV to OGG?
faqs.answer: Choose the WAV above and save the OGG when it's done. With several WAV files selected, each is encoded in order and saved on its own.

faqs.question: Is an OGG smaller than a WAV?
faqs.answer: Usually by a wide margin. Linear PCM, the common payload of a WAV, is stored uncompressed, while Vorbis is a lossy codec that gives up some of the sound to save space.

faqs.question: Is the OGG lossless?
faqs.answer: No. Vorbis is lossy, and the page encodes at quality 5. Keep the WAV if you may edit the recording again, since edits made from the OGG start with sound that has already been through lossy coding.

faqs.question: Does the page make an Opus file?
faqs.answer: No. It writes Vorbis audio in an Ogg container. The .ogg extension is conventionally for Vorbis, and .oga is the broader extension for Ogg audio.

faqs.question: Can I choose the bitrate?
faqs.answer: No. The page sets Vorbis quality 5 and offers no other setting. In quality mode the encoder chooses the bitrate.

faqs.question: Why do two OGG files of the same length differ in size?
faqs.answer: Quality-based encoding follows the sound. In a local test, five seconds of noise gave a much larger OGG than five seconds of a steady tone, so equal running times can give different file sizes.

faqs.question: What plays an OGG file?
faqs.answer: VLC, Audacity, Firefox and Chrome open OGG files. The container doesn't say which codec is inside, so a player needs the Vorbis decoder as well.

faqs.question: Do the title and artist tags come across?
faqs.answer: Usually. The page passes no option that removes tags, so FFmpeg copies the WAV's title, artist and similar tags to the OGG where it can hold them. In a local test a WAV's title and artist both came through.

faqs.question: Does a WAV always contain PCM?

guide.title: About WAV files
guide.markdown:
### What is a WAV file?

WAV, or WAVE, is a wrapper for sound built on RIFF, not one particular audio encoding. The format was set out by Microsoft and IBM in a multimedia specification dated August 1991. Linear PCM is the common payload, but compressed encodings can appear too, so the .wav ending alone doesn't tell you what is inside. The usual media-type labels are audio/wav and audio/x-wav. Broadcast WAVE extends the format with metadata for production and preservation, and the Library of Congress lists WAVE among its recommended formats for digital audio.

You come across WAV files from audio recorders, editing software and sound libraries: anywhere sound is kept untouched. The cost is size. An uncompressed recording takes far more space than a Vorbis copy of it, which is why many people look for a smaller file to send or store. The .wav ending also doesn't tell you whether a file holds plain PCM or something compressed.

### Programs that open WAV files

**Windows**

- Windows Media Player: opens WAV files.

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- Audacity: imports most WAV files, all PCM variants included.

**Web**

- Any web browser: plays a WAV with no extra software.

**Android, iOS, Linux, Mac and Windows**

- VLC media player: plays back WAV files.

### WAV and OGG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .wav uses audio/wav or audio/x-wav. .ogg uses audio/ogg for an audio-only stream.
- **Container**: WAV is a RIFF wrapper. Ogg is Xiph.Org's open container, which supports sequential reading and writing, so it suits streaming. Its framing includes timestamps and error detection.
- **Codec**: a WAV usually holds linear PCM. An OGG usually holds Vorbis, while .oga is the broader extension for audio in Ogg.
- **Size**: PCM is uncompressed. Vorbis is lossy and much smaller.
- **Metadata**: WAV keeps INFO chunks or Broadcast WAVE fields, which store different information.
- **Standards**: the IETF registered the Ogg media types in September 2008.

Ogg is Xiph.Org's open container for compressed multimedia streams. It can interleave sound and video, and the codec decides how each stream is compressed, which is why a bare .ogg ending doesn't name an encoding on its own.

This page decodes the WAV and writes Vorbis at quality 5 into an Ogg container. It is a quality setting, not a bitrate, so the size follows the sound. The command sets no bitrate, sample rate or channel count of its own, only the quality.

The practical split is simple. Keep a WAV for anything you will edit again, archive or hand to someone who mixes it. Make an OGG for a copy you will listen to, share or stream, where a small file matters more than the last bit of detail. Because Vorbis has already discarded sound, converting an OGG back to WAV gives you a large file with the same reduced content, not the original recording.

### Other ways to convert WAV to OGG

- **Audacity (Windows, Mac, Linux):** open the WAV, choose File > Export Audio, pick Ogg Vorbis from the Format dropdown and choose a quality from 0 to 10. The default is 5.
- **FFmpeg (command line):** run `ffmpeg -i input.wav -c:a libvorbis -q:a 5 output.ogg`. The quality scale runs from -1 to 10.
- **oggenc (command line):** run `oggenc -q 5 -o output.ogg input.wav`. The tool comes in Xiph's vorbis-tools and reads raw, Wave or AIFF audio.

### Problems with WAV files

- **Audacity won't import the recording**: a recorder may use proprietary compression inside the WAV. Audacity recommends installing its FFmpeg library for those.
- **A very large recording**: WAV files past the original RIFF size limit need RF64.
- **The WAV plays in one program but not another**: WAV is a wrapper, so a player needs the decoder for whatever encoding sits inside it. Convert it here or open it in Audacity to find out.
- **The OGG sounds worse than the WAV**: Vorbis is lossy. Keep the WAV, or re-run from the original recording rather than from another lossy copy.
- **A device rejects the OGG**: it may expect Opus or another codec. The extension doesn't identify one, and RFC 5334 keeps .ogg for Vorbis audio and gives general audio and video other extensions, .oga and .ogv.
- **A damaged OGG**: the container detects damaged pages but can't rebuild missing audio. Convert again from the WAV.

guide.title: About WebM files
guide.markdown:
### What is a WebM file?

WebM is an open media format that the WebM Project promotes for delivery over the web. The container is based on Matroska, and the streams inside are VP8, VP9 or AV1 video with Vorbis or Opus audio. The project offers its technology on royalty-free terms, and the major browsers support the format.

Video files carry the media type video/webm. A WebM holding nothing but sound is labeled audio/webm, so a .webm file is not always a video.

Typical sources are web video, the recordings that browser-based screen recorders save, and short animated clips.

### Programs that open WebM files

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- The VLC media player reads Matroska-family media, though its codec support has to match the streams inside the WebM.
- FFplay ships with FFmpeg and plays WebM through FFmpeg's decoders, so which codecs work depends on how that copy was built.

**Web**

- Chrome, Firefox and Edge open WebM files directly.
- Safari 14.1 is where macOS gained WebM playback; the picture has to be VP8 or VP9 and the audio Vorbis.

**Mobile**

- Android and iPhone owners can use VLC for Android or VLC for iOS, which play local WebM files with VLC's own player rather than the system player.

### WebM and GIF compared

- **Names**: .webm goes with video/webm, and .gif with image/gif.
- **Kind of file**: WebM wraps video. CompuServe brought out GIF in 1987 as an image format that can store several images one after another.
- **Animation**: the GIF89a revision from July 1990 added the extensions for timing, comments, application data and transparency. Delays are counted in hundredths of a second, and a disposal setting decides how a later image sits on top of an earlier one.
- **Colors**: every GIF image picks its colors from a palette that tops out at 256 entries. WebM video has no such ceiling.
- **Compression**: GIF squeezes its images with LZW, which loses nothing. WebM depends on its video codecs.
- **Sound**: a WebM can carry Vorbis or Opus audio. The GIF this page writes holds one picture stream and no audio.
- **Transparency**: a single palette entry can be flagged as clear, and there is no partial opacity.
- **Repeat count**: a GIF keeps its repeat count in an application extension, and the file this page writes has it set to repeat forever.
- **Patents**: Unisys started asking for LZW license fees in 1994, and the last of those patents lapsed in 2004.
- **Support**: every major browser displays GIF.

For this pair the page writes 15 frames a second, shrinks anything above 480 px on its longer side, and sets the GIF to repeat. Frames flagged as interlaced are deinterlaced before they are scaled.

### Other ways to convert WebM to GIF

- **FFmpeg:** run `ffmpeg -i input.webm output.gif`. FFmpeg takes the output format from the .gif ending, the same pattern its documentation shows with `ffmpeg -i input.avi output.mp4`. A plain command like this skips the frame-rate, size and palette steps this page applies.
- **Gifski with FFmpeg:** run `ffmpeg -i input.webm frame%04d.png` to write one PNG per frame, then `gifski -o anim.gif frame*.png` to build the GIF. Gifski's documentation names `--width` and `--height` as the biggest levers for a smaller file, and `--quality` for lowering quality. Its site also shows `gifski --fps 10 --width 320 -o anim.gif video.mp4` for an MP4 source, where `--fps` sets the frame rate and a lower value gives a smaller file. On Windows, the frame pattern may need `%%04d`.

### Problems with WebM files

- **It plays in a browser but not in an editor**: playback depends on the video and audio codecs actually used, not on the .webm ending. Check which codecs the file really uses before blaming the container, then convert it here or open it in VLC.
- **Seeking is slow or jumpy**: without a cue index, a player gets less direct location information, so jumping to a point is less efficient. Re-saving the file in a video editor rebuilds it.
- **Safari won't play it**: releases before 14.1 predate WebM playback in Safari on macOS, so update the browser or use another one.
- **It holds only sound**: an audio-only WebM is labeled audio/webm and has no picture to show, so play it in VLC to check what is inside.

faqs.question: Does the WebM stay on my device?

faqs.question: Can I do a batch of WebM files?

guide.title: About WebM and MP3 files
guide.markdown:
### What is a WebM file?

Media for the web is what WebM is built for, and the WebM Project promotes it as an open format. It is based on Matroska and combines VP8 or VP9 video with Vorbis or Opus audio, with AV1 video also in use. The project provides the format's technology royalty-free. A WebM with video uses video/webm as its media type, and one that holds only sound uses audio/webm.

You usually meet WebM as a saved web video, a screen recording from a browser or a short animated clip. The sound is a separate stream inside the file, so a converter can take it out without touching the picture.

The files are made for delivery over the web. A missing cue index leaves a player with less direct location information, which makes seeking less efficient.

### Programs that open WebM files

**Windows, Mac, Linux, Android and iOS**

- VLC media player: reads Matroska-family media, provided its codecs match the streams in the file. The Android release carries over the desktop player's decoding features.

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- FFplay: plays WebM with FFmpeg's decoders.

**Mac**

- Safari: supports WebM from 14.1 onward, covering VP8, VP9 and Vorbis.

### WebM and MP3 compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .webm with video/webm (audio/webm for sound only), against .mp3 with audio/mpeg.
- **Container**: WebM is a Matroska subset that holds video, audio and more. MP3 is a single audio stream.
- **Codecs**: WebM audio is Vorbis or Opus, while MP3 is MPEG-1 Audio Layer III from ISO/IEC 11172-3.
- **Openness**: the WebM Project licenses its technology royalty-free. The MP3 patent licensing program ended in April 2017.
- **Metadata**: ID3 data inside the MP3 is where titles and other tags live.
- **Support**: MP3 plays on nearly every device. Vorbis and Opus in a WebM depend on the player's codecs.
- **Typical use**: WebM fits web video, browser screen recordings and animated clips; MP3 fits music libraries, podcasts and portable players.

The page runs FFmpeg with its video output off and LAME set to 192 kbps, a rate LAME reaches only for audio sampled at 32 kHz or above. In a run on a sample WebM, FFmpeg decoded Vorbis audio and wrote it as a new MP3 stream. Both formats are lossy, so the audio goes through compression a second time, and detail the WebM already dropped does not return.

The output is named after the WebM, with .mp3 in place of .webm. A batch converts one file after another, and each MP3 is saved separately. Nothing caps size or running time, and FFmpeg works on one thread. The page gives you no bitrate, track or quality options.

### Other ways to convert WebM to MP3

- **FFmpeg (Windows, Mac, Linux):** execute `ffmpeg -i input.webm -vn -c:a libmp3lame output.mp3`. -vn turns the video off.
- **Audacity with FFmpeg (Windows, Mac, Linux):** Audacity can import the sound of most video files other than DRM-protected ones provided the optional FFmpeg library is installed. Then open the WebM, go to File > Export Audio and choose MP3 in the Format menu.

FFmpeg's b option sets a bitrate of your own, for example -b:a 192k, and Audacity's export dialog has MP3 options, so both desktop routes offer what this page does not.

### Problems with WebM files

- **An error or a silent result**: the WebM may have no audio track. Play it first to check.
- **Plays in one program but not another**: playback depends on the real video and audio codecs, not on the .webm ending.
- **The bitrate is lower than expected**: a WebM with 16 to 24 kHz audio gets at most 160 kbps from LAME, and one at 8 to 12 kHz gets 64 kbps.
- **The recording is cut short**: a damaged or truncated WebM often converts anyway, giving a shorter MP3.
- **Seeking is sluggish**: a WebM missing its cue index gives players less to seek with.
- **Older Safari will not play it**: releases before 14.1 on macOS lack WebM support.
- **A renamed file fails**: changing .webm to .mp3 leaves the Matroska data inside. Convert the file instead.
- **Titles are missing in the MP3**: FFmpeg carries the WebM's global tags, for example title and artist, into the MP3 when it has them. Add the rest with a tag editor.

guide.title: About WebP and ICO
guide.markdown:
### What is a WebP file?

WebP is an image format developed by Google and released as open source. Google announced it on 30 September 2010. Its lossy compression is based on VP8, the video codec Google released as open source in May 2010, and applies VP8's intra-frame coding to still images. The lossless variant takes another route, combining LZ77 matching, prefix codes and a color cache. A WebP file is a RIFF container.

Transparency and animation work in both lossy and lossless WebP, and the file can also store an ICC profile along with Exif and XMP metadata. An image can be at most 16,383 x 16,383 pixels. On average, Google says lossless WebP comes out about 26% smaller than PNG, and lossy WebP about 30% smaller than JPEG. WebP was documented in RFC 9649 in November 2024, which also registers the image/webp media type.

### Programs that open WebP files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP handles WebP import and export natively as of version 2.10.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** ImageMagick reads WebP; inspect `magick identify -list format` for your installed build.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** XnView MP reads and writes WebP, and is free for private or educational use. A company needs a license.
- **Windows and Mac:** Photoshop reads and writes WebP without a plug-in from version 23.2.
- **Windows:** With Microsoft's WebP Image Extension installed, File Explorer and Photos can open WebP images.
- **Web:** Firefox and Chrome display WebP, though older versions may not animate it. Lossy WebP displays in Chrome 17+, Edge 18+, Firefox 65+ and Safari 14+.
- **Mobile:** Safari on iPhone and Chrome on Android display WebP. Android decodes WebP from version 4.0, and lossless or transparent WebP from 4.2.1.

### WebP and ICO compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .webp is image/webp. .ico is image/vnd.microsoft.icon.
- **Purpose**: WebP is a web image format. Microsoft designed ICO for icons in graphical interfaces, and the .ico extension is best known today from website favicons.
- **Several images**: an ICO file may contain more than one image. A WebP is one picture, or one animation.
- **Animation**: WebP can animate. The ICO written here holds one still image.
- **Transparency**: both formats support an alpha channel.
- **Size**: a WebP can be up to 16,383 px a side. ICO stores each side in one byte, so an image tops out at 256 px.
- **Byte order**: ICO files use little-endian byte ordering.

Windows Vista icon guidance includes 256-by-256 images for high-DPI displays, which is where the 256 px limit sits. On this page, the browser's own decoder reads the WebP and ImageMagick writes the ICO. Only one image goes in. A larger picture is fitted down to the limit, and one that is already smaller keeps its size. At 256 px the image is embedded in the ICO as PNG data. Metadata isn't copied.

### Other ways to convert WebP to ICO

- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux):** open the WebP and choose File > Export As. Change the Name field's extension to .ico, or pick ICO under Select File Type, then export. The ICO dialog sets the color depth and offers a Compressed (PNG) checkbox.
- **Pillow (Python):** open the WebP with `Image.open` and call `save` with a .ico filename. Pass `sizes=[(16,16),(32,32),(48,48)]` to put several icon sizes in one file. The default is 16, 24, 32, 48, 64, 128 and 256 px, and any size bigger than the original or 256 is ignored. Pillow needs libwebp to read WebP.
- **FFmpeg (command line):** run `ffmpeg -i input.webp output.ico`. FFmpeg's documentation lists WebP among the image formats it decodes and ICO among the formats it reads and writes.

### Problems with WebP files

- **Older browsers and animation**: an old browser may show a still WebP yet be unable to play an animated one.
- **A WebP beyond 16,383 px**: WebP caps each side at 16,383 pixels, so a bigger image runs past the format's limit.
- **A tool can't read the WebP**: a given ImageMagick install might lack WebP decoding or encoding, so look in its format list.
- **The page says it can't open the file**: you see "This browser can't open ... files" when your browser has no WebP decoder, and "Image decode failed." for a file the browser can't read. Updating to a current Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari cures the first.

guide.title: About WebP files
guide.markdown:
### What is a WebP file?

WebP is a Google-made image format, open source from the start. The announcement came on 30 September 2010. In lossy mode, WebP applies the intra-frame coding of VP8, a video codec that began at On2 Technologies and that Google released as open source in May 2010. The VP8 specification, RFC 6386, is built around On2's own reference decoder. A lossless mode with its own method followed, and both modes can carry transparency and animation. Inside, a WebP is a RIFF container. RFC 9649, published in November 2024, documents the format and registers its media type, image/webp.

You mostly meet WebP on the web. Google reports lossy WebP files about 30% smaller than JPEG on average, and lossless WebP files about 26% smaller than PNG. Animated WebP turns up too: WhatsApp's animated stickers, for example, are WebP files.

### Programs that open WebP files

- **Windows:** File Explorer and Photos open WebP once Microsoft's WebP Image Extension is installed.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP reads and writes WebP natively, since version 2.10. ImageMagick reads WebP, and its format list shows whether your installation can.
- **Web and mobile:** Google Chrome displays WebP.
- **Web:** Mozilla Firefox displays WebP, and so does Microsoft Edge.
- **Mac and mobile:** Safari shows WebP from macOS Big Sur and iOS 14.
- **Mobile:** On Android, WebP displays from version 4.0, with lossless and transparent files supported from 4.2.1.

Adobe Photoshop handles WebP files natively as well, starting with version 23.2.

### WebP and JPG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .webp and image/webp; .jpg or .jpeg and image/jpeg.
- **Compression**: lossy WebP codes the picture as a VP8 key frame, and lossless WebP uses LZ77, prefix codes and a color cache. Baseline JPEG is always lossy: 8x8 blocks, a discrete cosine transform, then Huffman coding.
- **Transparency**: WebP has an alpha channel in both modes. JPG has none.
- **Animation**: WebP can hold timed frames. A JPG is one still picture.
- **Color depth**: JPEG keeps 8 bits per channel. The page converts through 8-bit RGBA pixels, so a deeper source loses its extra bits.
- **Largest image**: a WebP side tops out at 16,383 pixels.
- **Quality setting**: Most programs ask for a JPEG quality from 0 to 100, but one value gives different results in different tools. This page has no setting and uses 0.85 for every file.
- **Layers and progressive mode**: JPEG cannot store layers. A progressive JPEG shows a rough preview that sharpens as the rest arrives.
- **Reach**: JPEG opens in all the major browsers, and cameras and scanners commonly save it. Safari 14, Firefox 65, Edge 18 and Chrome 17, along with later releases, show lossy WebP, and elsewhere WebP needs one of the programs above.
- **Metadata**: WebP can carry an ICC profile, Exif and XMP. The JPG made here carries none of them.

The change here is the move to a format without transparency or animation. The page decodes the WebP to pixels and writes a JPG at quality 0.85. See-through areas can't stay see-through, an animation gives its first frame, and the Exif, ICC profile and XMP aren't copied.

### Other ways to convert WebP to JPG

- **GIMP (Windows, Mac and Linux):** open the WebP in GIMP 2.10 or later, then export it as a JPEG from File > Export As.
- **ImageMagick (terminal):** run `magick input.webp output.jpg`, if the installation can read WebP.

### Problems with WebP files

- **Double-clicking does nothing on Windows**: install the WebP Image Extension from the Microsoft Store.
- **An older browser shows nothing**: Edge 18, Chrome 17, Firefox 65 and Safari 14 were the first to show lossy WebP, so earlier releases can't display it.
- **A site or form rejects it**: convert it to JPG here, or to PNG with the [WebP to PNG converter](/webp-to-png/) when transparency must survive.
- **A renamed file still fails**: changing .webp to .jpg leaves WebP data inside. Convert the file instead.
- **Only one frame came out**: a JPG can't animate, so an animated WebP gives its first frame. Keep the WebP if you need the motion.
- **"Image decode failed."**: the browser's decoder couldn't read the file. Download it again from where you found it.
- **The JPG looks soft or blotchy**: a lossy WebP has already lost some detail, and the JPG is compressed again on top. Start from the largest, least compressed copy the site offers.

guide.title: About WebP files
guide.markdown:
### What is a WebP file?

Google created WebP for images on the web. The lossy mode is built on the VP8 video codec, and the format also covers lossless compression, alpha transparency and animation. A WebP image can't be larger than 16,383 pixels on either axis. The file is a RIFF container. Lossy files apply VP8 intra-frame coding, whereas lossless files rely on a distinct method that combines LZ77, prefix codes and a color cache. Its image/webp media type comes from RFC 9649, which describes the format. Room exists inside a file for Exif and XMP metadata and an ICC color profile.

PDF has a different job. A form, a portal or a colleague may ask for a document when all you have is one image. Putting the WebP on a PDF page gives them something any PDF reader can open and print. The conversion does not recover the page the picture came from, and it adds no text. It also doesn't change the picture: you can still look at the WebP you started with, and the PDF is a second copy for the cases where a document is required.

### Programs that open WebP files

**Android**

- Android: it decodes WebP from version 4.0, but lossless or transparent files wait until 4.2.1.

**Mac and iPhone**

- Safari: opens WebP from version 14, on macOS Big Sur and iOS 14 onward.

**Windows**

- File Explorer and Photos: Microsoft's WebP Image Extension has to be installed before they show WebP images.

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- GIMP: native WebP import and export arrived in GIMP 2.10.
- ImageMagick: reads WebP and writes PDF, which makes it a command-line route between the two.

### WebP and PDF compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .webp is image/webp, and .pdf is application/pdf.
- **What they hold**: a WebP is one image, or an animation. A PDF is a document with pages, which can contain images, text and vector drawings. PDF is standardized as ISO 32000.
- **Compression**: WebP is lossy or lossless. The PDF made here stores the decoded pixels as lossless PNG data.
- **Transparency**: WebP has an alpha channel. The PDF keeps it as a soft mask, and no background is added behind the picture.
- **Animation**: WebP can animate, and a PDF page can't. You get the first frame.
- **Layout**: a PDF has fixed pages. This one has a single page sized to the image. It has no margins and isn't set to A4 or Letter.
- **Text**: a picture inside a PDF stays a picture. Selectable text needs a separate OCR step.

The browser decodes the WebP, and the page embeds the pixels without a second lossy step. The pixels travel as 8-bit RGBA, which is why EXIF, ICC and XMP data don't make it into the PDF. Each file you pick is converted on its own.

### Other ways to convert WebP to PDF

- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux):** load the WebP, pick File > Export As, and choose the .pdf extension or the PDF file type. In GIMP's PDF dialog, an option can replace transparent areas with the background color, so check it when transparency matters.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick input.webp output.pdf`. On a 96 by 96 pixel test image it wrote a 96 by 96 point page.
- **Pillow (Python):** run `python3 -c "from PIL import Image; Image.open('input.webp').convert('RGB').save('output.pdf')"`. Pillow writes an RGB image into a PDF with JPEG encoding, so the picture is compressed again and loses its transparency.

### Problems with WebP files

- **The PDF prints at a surprising size**: pixels are not paper. A page with one point per pixel can be much larger than Letter or A4.
- **Several files downloaded**: each WebP you select makes its own PDF. Combine them afterward if you need one document.
- **The text can't be selected**: lettering in the picture is still image pixels, and the PDF adds no text layer.
- **A moving image became still**: only the first frame of an animated WebP is used. Keep the WebP for the animation.
- **A picture over 16,383 pixels**: WebP cannot be larger than that on either axis, so such a file points to a broken download or another format. Fetch it again.
- **The image won't load**: your browser decodes the WebP, so an old browser without WebP support can't open it.

- ImageMagick: reads WebP, if your installation includes the format.
- XnView MP: reads and writes WebP; free for private or educational use.

**Web**

- Lossy WebP shows in Chrome from version 17, Edge from 18, Firefox from 65 and Safari from 14.

**Mobile**

- On Android, WebP decodes from version 4.0, with lossless or transparent files from 4.2.1. iPhone Safari shows it from iOS 14.

### WebP and SVG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .webp with image/webp; .svg with image/svg+xml.
- **What they store**: WebP stores pixels. SVG is written in XML and describes shapes, text and embedded images, which means one SVG can hold drawn artwork or just a picture.
- **Scaling**: a vector SVG stays sharp at any size. A pixel image does not, and neither does an SVG that merely wraps one.
- **Animation**: WebP can hold timed frames. An SVG can animate through CSS or scripts, but that is a different mechanism.
- **Text**: an SVG is plain text, so it can be edited in a text editor and searched, indexed and compressed. A WebP is a RIFF container.
- **Linked pictures**: an SVG can point to a picture in another file and lose it when that file is unavailable. This page avoids that by embedding the picture inside the SVG itself.

This is what the conversion does. The page decodes the WebP and writes an SVG that contains a single image element: your picture, embedded as a base64 PNG, at the picture's own width and height. Nothing is traced into paths. The SVG opens wherever SVG opens, but it scales like the original bitmap, and its colors and shapes can't be edited as objects.

### Other ways to convert WebP to SVG

These routes trace the picture into paths, which is a different job from the embedding this page does. dwebp does not read animated WebP files.

- **Inkscape with dwebp:** run `dwebp input.webp -o input.png`, which writes a PNG. In Inkscape choose File > Import, select the image with the Selector tool, then choose Path > Trace Bitmap, set the options and click OK. Tracing is not a faithful copy, and color tracing makes one object per color, which can be hard to edit.
- **Potrace with dwebp:** run `dwebp input.webp -bmp -o input.bmp`, which writes an uncompressed BMP, then `potrace -s input.bmp -o output.svg`. Potrace reads PBM, PGM, PPM and BMP, and -s selects the SVG backend.

### Problems with WebP files

- **Renaming the file doesn't work**: changing .webp to .svg leaves WebP data inside, and an SVG has to be XML text.
- **It won't open in an older program**: install Microsoft's WebP Image Extension on Windows, or use a recent browser, GIMP or Photoshop.
- **A design tool rejects it**: turn the WebP into a plain bitmap with the [WebP to PNG converter](/webp-to-png/), then bring that in.
- **An old browser shows a still**: an older browser can show a still WebP yet lack animation support. On this page an animated WebP gives its first frame only.
- **The picture is too big for WebP**: WebP limits each side to 16,383 pixels, so a file claiming more is damaged or not a WebP.
- **A decode failure message appears**: the browser could not open the file. Try an up-to-date Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari, or fetch a fresh copy.
- **ImageMagick can't read it**: a WebP decode or encode may be unavailable in a particular installation, so check its format list.
